During the year juss ended the House of Com- mons has lost twelve members—Mr. Christopher Talbot, Mr. Craig-Sellar, Mr. Joseph Biggar, Mr. Swetenham,Q.C., Mr. Matthew Harris, Mr. Handel Cossfiam, Mr. W. Crawford, Mr. David Pugh, Mr. .Marum, Mr. W. Beckett, Mr. Egerton, and Mr. Thomas Richardson.

The cadse of the failure cf Anton Rubinstein's eyesight is said to be persistent smoking while at the pianoforte. His sight has now become so bad that it is likely to necessitate his retirement from public life. Rubinstein is a great smoker, and he is probably not the first musician who has injured his eyes beyond recovery with tobacco smoke.

The Prince of Wales's kennels and the Prince of Wales's dogs have got a Christmas number. all to themselves in the shape of a supplement to the, "Stock Keeper," which is profusely illustrated. The Sandringham kennels are a fine row of buildings which will bear comparison with some of the best modern houses in the Zoo, and are venk jar ahead of the average dwellings of the people IN East Lon- don.

OPPOSED TO PROTECTION. • He sees plainly that it benefits and protects only the Trust and the Syndicate. Employers become millionares by its help, while paying their workmen mere starvation wages. The fact is, there can be no protection for the workmen, so long as Europe and Asia pour their surplus population into American cities. In my own trade there are at least three meü for every job, and I know this is title state of things all round, and yet agents are now travelling through Europe picturing America as a very' El Dorado.' The Tariff Bill.has caused quite a sensa- tion here. Its effect has been immediate : the store- keepers at once took advantage of its provisions. One of my daughters purchasing a yard of velvet for trimming, paid two dollars for what, the week previous, would have cost a clonal and a quarter. This was 3s. extra on a yard of velvet. All kinds of soft goods of the cheaper grades have gone up in price considerably; far more, comparatively, than the higher grade articles. I look upon the measure as a reduction in my wages of at least a dollar a week; I have heard nothing yet from the employer as to an increase in our price list. Lady Dilke patronised the match girls on Mon- day night, and gave them .sound advice on trade unionism. She believes in a defensive unionism— the creation of a strong combination among the workers which would better their condition. Lady Dilke "expressed her decided disapproval of strikes," and although it was a strike which made the Matchgirls' Union, they are likely to agree with her, for a strike would just as easily unmake it.

Lord Derby has been talking again on the solution of the social problem. He considers that "with an increasing population of four hundred thousand year, emigration is the only palliative. It is the "swarms of the lowest class" whom Lord Derby would export. But where is he going to find room for them all? America will not take paupers of the lowest class; Canada does not want them. Australia has no room for them at present, and other eligible portions of the globe are getting filled up.

A writer of exquisite verse, too little read by the contemporaries of Mr. Swinburne, furnishes a quotation singularly appropriate to Mr. Gladstone's birthday. In him Demosthenes was heard again; Liberty taught him her Athenian strain; She clothed him with authority and awe, Spoke from his lips, and in his looks gave law. His speech, his form, his action, full of grace, And all his country beaming in his face, He stood as some inimitable hand Would strive to make a Paul or Tully stand. No sycophant or slave, that dared oppose Her sacred cause, but trembled when he rose; And every venal stickler for the yoke Felt himself crushed at the first word he spoke.

don't see why a, simple p—rohibiiion measure was not placed on the statute book. It would have been effectual as a Chinese wall, allowing only British gold to come in as payment for American food pro- ducts, of which the English market is the largest in the world. Of course the American politician ignores the ordinary rules of commerce : he. is a law unto himself. But the politician isn't everybody: the common people count, once in a way, and the fall elections have just proved that they count effectually when they once set about it. All the same, in spite of the change which has passed over the people's opinions, the McKinley Bill MUST STAND AS LAW

Mr. Alfred Cattertnole. agent for the Liberals in one of the divisions of Bassetlaw, is a man of infi- nite resource. The Sunday before the election he went to the Wesleyan Chapel, and was surprised by a visit from the stewards, who told him that the minister had failed to put in an appearance, and it was the unanimous desire of the congregation that he should preach the sermon. Nothing abashed, the agent ascended the pulpit, aild preached an ex- cellent discourse. It was not, we are told, political. Mr. Cattermole is one of Mr. Schnadhorst's favourite pupils, and evidently deserves to be.

The "Century" has made a great success by securing Talleyrand's Memoirs as it did with "The Life of Lincoln.' It is expanding from a magazine into a publishing business. The works which now appear month by month in its pages are not confined to stories. Lincoln's Life, which will soon be .pub- lished in this country by Mr. Fisher Unwin, is a great standard work of history of seven volumes. Jefferson's Autobiography was also a great, success, but Talleyrand's Memoirs is a work which will awaken more cosmopolitan interest than either of the two books mentioned.

The following letter, written at the request of the Queen, has naturally given much pleasure to the Welsh folks at Denbigh. It appears that a weaver, Mr. Edward Williams, of Henllan-street in that town sent, through Mrs. Mainwaring, a Welsh home-shun petticoat to the Queen. The Dowager Lady Churchill. as Lady-in-Waiting, has sent the following acknowledgment from Windsor Castle : —" I have found the petticoat on my arrival ihere. It is a very nice one. I have given it to the Queen who is much pleased with it. Will you say to the weaver that the Queen is much obliged to hiin for having sent it tiiher, and her Majesty likes it very much:"

Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., is generally believed to rejoice in the sound of his own voice, and an illus:- tration of this weakness is going the rounds of the Midlands. The Rev. W. Tuckwell was announced to address a meeting at which Mr. Jesse Collings was to preside. The meeting assembled, the chair- man rose to make " a few brief remarks,' and talked on for one hour and twenty minutes. Then he called upon the Radical parson, who was equal to the occasion, and moving. That the best thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. Jesse Collings for his eloquent address," resumed his seat. The audience entered into the spirit of the thing, and "made the welkin ring" With laughter.

It is a long time since a Tory Premier has had a chance of nominating an archbishop, and of all the plums in the way of ecclesiastical patronage which have fallen to Lord Salisbury, the Archbishopric of York is by tar the greatest. Since the present Government has been in power, Lord Salisbury has nominated to the sees of Manchester, Wakefield, Chester, St. Asaph, Durham, Winchester, Bangor, Worcester, St. Albans, and Rochester. Amongst those mentioned as probable successor of Archbis- hop Thomson are Dr. Wilkinson, of Truro, a High Churchman; Bishop Westcott, who, it is said, will not accept the position, and Bishops Magee, Good- win, Carpenter, and Moorhouse.

The French Government has always an eye on nest sources of taxation. They have now pounced on the great industry of gambling, by resolving to tax clubs. Clubs in Paris do not resemble the National Liberal Club or the Athenmum. They ara betting and gambling institutions. Money won at the roulette table, or on betting, is as legitimate a source oi taxation as ground rents. But the diffi- culty which the Government had to face was how to get the gamblers to declare :their gains. They taxed the club manager at the rate of twenty per cent. on the total resources of the club several years ago, but the managers understated their income. The law has been changed, and now clubs are to be taxed at the rate of five to twenty per cent. on members' subscriptions, and from two to eight per cent, on the rent at the clubhouse.

At this bitter season, when the youngest and the strongest constitutions require all the help. that food and warmth and clothing can give, it is in- structive to read of a contrast such as this. At the inquest on Emma Mills who died of want at St. George's-in-the-East, the doctor deposed that the only signs of food which he could discover in the house were" some pieces of dry bread which had evidently been picked out of the gutter." At an inquest in St. Pancras the widow' stated that she and her husband had long lived on half a crown a week. "She did not want much to eat, and had lived on a piece of dry bread a day." So much for one side of the medal. On the other may suitably be engraved this excerpt from the account of a dinner party in a provincial paper:—" There were ten of them present, and the dinner cost .2300." Cela donne ri penser.

for at least two Years more. The Senate, which may be compared to the British House of Lords as a privileged obstructive body, are all rich, very rich men, and take every measure for keeping them- selves a compact law-making clique. One of their number, Senator Stanford, during the election just past, spent thousands of dollars bribing voters. His myrmidons stood at street corners with tickets • ready signed and folded offering 19s. to every voter willing to take it. By this means California' re- turned Republicans to the State.A.ssembly, Stanford thus making sure of his return to the Senate. Law proceedings have been taken against this man, but he claimed Senatorial privilege for defying the courts. The Court sat for two hours, but the big man never showed • up. The American Senate is about the biggest swindling body in existence : as rich men they act in collusion with Wall-st. ; they work hand in hand with every Syndicate and Trust. While Mr. McKinley's committee was at work pre- paring the new law it Was aided by the constant advice and assistance of the representatives of scores of Trusts; but can anybody point out a line , in the Act that was inserted at the request of a de- legation of working-men? I wish to deal fully with this question of Pro- tection, because, although I well know there is no chance for it again in England, there are quite a number of people who have a sort of sneaking love for this thing, and who may ,now think it time to be up and doing, if it be only to give the Yankee a rap on the knuckles. Ex-Consul Hale, who, from his long residence in Manchester, should know some- thing of international commerce, says that "high protective tariff in the United States simply re- leased to the manufactures ofl 'Great Britain all the neutral markets of the world." Speaking as to quality of goods, Mr. Hale says further : I had often wondered why clothing materials manufac- tured in America were not equal in quality and dura- bility to those manufactured abroad,until the cause was explained to me by Englishmen. Under a high ,protective tariff the manufacturer can be careless in manufacturing because he knows that he can always sell poor and shoddy clothing, and as long as he is assured of this he will refuse to make better clothing. If he were forced into competition ' with the rest of the world he would manufacture ' good clothing and the consumer would be bene- fited. I think lam showing to your readers THE HIGH WAGE FALLACY,

and. by the way, very low wages . prevail in most trades throughout the Eastern States. It may be thought that what Mr. Hale says, and what I have said in your columns, touching the quality of American manufactured goods may not be quite re- liable. I have evidence before me gathered from all sources as to its truth. As a family man I know its truth too intimately. A hard felt hat that at home cost about 3s. here costs from 12s. to 16s. The same applies all round. Does Protection keep wages tip? 1 have before me quite a long list of firms reducing wiges. At Lowell (Mass.), Lynn (Mass.), Ashland (Penn.), wages have gone down all round. The Ohio Iron and Steel Co. have reduced. Strikes are on at the great iron mines in Michigan. The Pitts- burg and Lake Angeline Co. have all their men out. This company is said to have cleared a profit last year equal to its entire capital stock, 1 want it to be noticed that big profits and high wages do not go together. Lack of foreign competition gives the power to the syndicates which can virtually, and do, say—" Take the wages we offer, or starve ; no foreigner can interfere with us." A third party is coming rapidly to the front, and their voice will have to be listened to. Hitherto the farmers have been Republican and Protectionists; they are now beginning to see their mistake. All they buy is at Protection prices; what they sell has to compete with other food-growing countries on the British exchange.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAMRDAY, JANUARY 3, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAMRDAY, JANUARY 3, 1891.
THE McKINLEY BILL.
BY H. WHITHAM.

To Reformers the passing of the McKinley Tariff Bill is a great blow. Years ago it was strongly hoped by Englishmen that the American war tax, a tax imposed for the raising of the sinews of war, would be repealed at an early date, but it almost appears as if to-day the consummation of this wish were as far off as ever. Yet there are those who

think they see in this last effort of Protection but the beginning of the end. lam strongly of this opinion myself. I think I hear amongst the work- men I converse with such mumblings and grumbl- ings touching Protection as must soon affect the commercial policy of the ruling party in America. "Bossism," which knows no political principle, has so corrupted politics that the large majority of the workmen who engage in the political struggles have not the least idea as to what the science of life may be. They are mere tools, for live dollars a day, of a class whoare not workmen, but are merely well dressed hoodlums who gain a living by exploit- ing everybody and everything, and are well paid by the party organization. I remember one or two of my friends saying before 1 left home, "Well, you won't be ling in America before you become a Protectionist. lam not got down to that yet, nor lam I likely. What I see of its workings here convinces me of its great immora- lity. It encourages crime of the deepest dye, that of taking every mean advantage of the toilers. And yet I am not of the Manchester heartless and soulless schools. Often competition and protection alike are no friends to the workman. They are the millstones between which he is ground. For the present I know my position is impractical, but— "wait a little longer.'

I wish to say my health is a little better just now. lam only troubled with a strained hand and wrist: and a foot upon which a lump of iron fell. This past year has been rather a hard one for us ; but as my old friend Norbury used to say "never mind." A Merry Christmas to us all. 810, Bay St., San Francisco, Dec. 6, 1890.
THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW; OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.

div.head: CHAPTER XL
div.p: CHAPTER XL

AN ASTOUNDING AFFAIR. Half an hour had the gun-maker sat by the side of the sick mar.'s bed, when he was aroused from the reverie into which he had fallen by the gentle opening of the door. He turned and beheld a human form emerging from the narrow, dark, entryway. As it came into the room the watcher started, for he beheld the humpbacked priest, Savotano. "Who is here ?" the arch fiend whispered, shad- ing his eyes and trying to peer into the gloom. " ----sh !" uttered Ruric. " The count is
_ asleep." By this time our hero had so far overcome the first emotion caused by the villian's entrance that he could be calm.

"And who is this ?" the priest whispered, moving nearer to the bed. "Ha ! The gun-maker !" "Yes," replied the youth,watching every look and movement of the fellow most closely. "You are in a strange place, I should say," Savo- tano whispered, not looking the young man directly in the face, but casting upon nim a sidelong glance, as though he dared not look direct.

" Speak not too loud, sir priest," said our hero, de- termined to enter into no conversation with the man if he could avoid it. "Do not awaken the count, for he is very faint and weak." And then Ruric had another reason! He feared if Damonoff should awake, that the strange discovery they had made might be revealed, and of course he wished not that the villain should yet know how well he was understood.

"But why are you here ?" pursued Savotano, who seemed determined to know. "I am this poor man's spiritual comforter, and I surely have a right to know wherefore is the presence of one bearing the peculiar relations towards him which are sustained by you." Ruric's first impulse wasnone of disgust and wrath, but he managed to keep it to himself. "Sir priest," he returned, moving his chair noise- lessly nearer to the visitor, so that his: whisper might not disturb the sleeper, "I heard that the count was dying, and I would not have him die .without first forgiving me for all that I had done." "And has he done it ?" " He has." "And why do you remain here? Where is his attendant ?i; "She is out somewhere. The count has had a strange fit—a startling spasm—and I feared if he had another the woman could not manage him alone." " Ah," uttered Savotano. "A spasm ?" " Yes—a most strange one—as though something were at his heart—as though his brain were on fire, and his whole system shaking." The priest turned his head away, but Runic saw plainly the exultant !ook which rested there. There was no mistaking any more. That one look—for Runic saw it—was proof enough. " Well, well," the misshapen villain said, " I will I call again when he is awake. I would not have him die, and I nut by him." Thus speaking Savotano arose and moved towards the door. His step was eager, and his every. look betrayed some anxious purpose. He stopped as he reached the door and looked back, but he did not speak. Runic was afraid he might go to the side- board to look at the medicine, but he did not. He simply cast one more glance at, the watcher, and then left the room. In half an hour more the surgeon returned. His face wore a clear,emphatic expression,and his move- ments were all quick and prompt, as though each one was for the purpose of announcing some self- evident decision. "Well," he uttered, with a quickly drawn breath, "we have put the medicines to a test." And then he leaned back and looked into Rune's face. "And what did you find ?" the young man asked. "Just what we had expected. We have detected arsenic in three of the medicines which the Count had to take; but this poision is not alone. There is much opium in the wine, even so that We could smell it when our suspicions guided us. The poison has been most adroitly fixed. The priest must have one of those receipts which have been used by scientific poisoners, for no physician in Moscow could have concocted the deadly potion. "But wherein was it so wondrously peculiar ?' asked Runic with interest. "Why—in this :Arsenic was theprincipal poison- Ina agent, but that alone would produce symptoms which any physician would know at once. In this case there was something present which overcame all the outward signs of the poison, and only let it eat upon the vitals. I know not the secret, though I know there is such an one. Had it not been for your fortunate suspicions the count would have died from the effects of the wound. The poison was working silently, and surely—without pain, and without outward sign different from the usual sink- ing of the worn and fainting body. But I have hopes now. The villain must not know that we have discovered him. We will let the thing run for the present." Kopani was not a little surprised when he found that the priest had been there during his absence, but before he could make any further remark the count awoke. Helelt very faint but that strange sickness of the stomach was lessened. The surgeon prepared some suitable diluents, and having called in the woman he gave directions that they should be given in large quantities; and also directed her to prepare some strong barley water for the patient to drink as he wanted beverage. All the phials were replacei upon the sideboard, aUd then refilled with liquids somewhat like those they had before contained ; but the nurse was directed not to use them. Everything that her patient was to take she was to keep under her own charge in the kitchen; and she was also most par- ticularly cautioned against allowing the priest to gain anything from her. But Kopani meant to be sure on that score. He had a little business to transact, and then he was coming back to spend the night himself by the count's side. He meant at all events, that the poisoner should have no more op- portunity to exercise his diabolical scienee upon the sick nobleman. He promised the count that he should have safe and competent watchers there- after. It was fairly dark now, 'as Runic could see by raising the curtain and looking out. He had no idea it was so late. Time had passed without his notice. He moved to the side of the bed and took the invalid's hand. "I must go now," he said, "but if you are wil- ling, I will come again--" "You will come," uttered Conrad, in reply, re- turning the grasp of the hand with all his feeble power. "Oh, you must come often now. I hope I shall live. Perhaps I shall. If I do, I shall owe my life to you. And God knows—for the feeling is even now firm in my soul—that I will never think, never, of the sad blow you struck me. Come ,---come to me when you can, for now—now—as God lives I speak the truth—now I love you !" "God bless and keep you," murmured Rune, in a husky, tremulous voice; and with these words, coming from th very Apths of his soul, he turned away and left the room. He heard the voice of the count as he moved towards the open door, and thanked God that 'twas a blessing which fell upon his ears. Alt, those who know not what true forgivenness is, know not what is thepoliest emotion on earth! Runic had left his sledge• at a neighbouring inn, and as soon as he gained the street lus bent his I steps that way. He had gone half the distance ' from the residence of the count to the inn, and was just upon the point of crossing the street, when he heard his name pronounced by some one behind him. He stopped and looked around, and saw a man approaching him. It was too dark to distinguish faces plainly, even at a usual conversational distance; yet Runic was I not long in concluding that the man who had thus hailed him was a stranger. He was a medium- sized man, and so closely enveloped in his bonnet and pelisse that his form and features would have been hidden even had it been lighter than it was.

"Did you speak to me ?" asked the youth, as the man came up. "Yes, sir. Is your name Ruric Nevel ?" "It is." "Then you are wanted a few moments at the raj- denee of a lieutenant, named Orsa," "'Alaric Orsa ?" asked Ruric. "The same." "But he does not live here in the Kremlin." '"He is herd now, at any rate, and would see you." •_ _ _

"But you said he was at his residence "suggested our hero, who was fearful that some evil might be meant for him. "I know nothing to the contrary sir," the stranger returned, promptly. "All I can say is'

div.head: LON ING MOTHER'S LAST SHILLING.
div.p: THE LON ING MOTHER'S LAST SHILLING.
One night in the spring of 1886 Mrs. McPhee was

sitting in her humble home in Glasgow. It was nearly time for her son, David, to be back from his work, and she was anxiously expecting him. Indeed her mini was full of sad thoughts about the condition of her family and herself. Her husband, who was a card grinder and employed at the Oak Bank Mill, Glasgow, for more than ten years, had died at 1882, leaving three children for her to take care of as best she could. He had long been in ill-health, and could only make eighteen shillings a week, and it kept them very poor. When at last he died there was no one left to earn bread for the family except David, then a lad of thirteen, and feeble and ailing at that. Eight years had passed since then, and by God's mercy they have somehow lived and kept to- gether. While recalling these things Mrs. McPhee suddenly heard a sound as of somebody fumbling at the door and trying to enter. She went to the door and opened it, when who should come staggering in but David, looking so wan and exhausted that, as she says, she "expected to see him fall dead at her feet." All through that fearsome night he lay in great agony. His loving mother nursed him faithfully, without resting or sleeping a moment. She gave him some medicine they chanced to have in the house, and applied hot flannels and fomentations.. If anything were needed to make the poor woman toil harder to save him it was the terrible thought, "What if David should be taken away I What then would be- come of his poor old mother and the children? for he is our bread-winner and all we have." In the morning he was a very little better, and the mother went to a doctor in Cowcaddens Street, who prescribed some medicine and a blister plaster. This, David afterwards said, eased him a little, but reft him so weak he could scarcely crawl.
The good lad got back to his work, but he was a piti- ful sight to see. Yet he bravely stuck to his work for the sake of his dear mother and the younger chit- . dr en . _ _

Only a few weeks ago, however, it was that David told the story which throws light on the event we have just described. He says: "I am twenty-one years old, and am at present employed at :an Agricultural imple- ment Works, Cattle Market in this city, Glasgow. I was weak and sickly from childhood. About five years ago I began to feel very bad. I could take no food that agreed with me, and had great pain after eating. I had a nasty,. sticky taste in my mouth all 'slay long, but worst in the morning, and a strange, sinking feeling at the pit of my stomach. Although I craved food it did not satisfy me, but only caused me distress. I was then working at Woodsaid's Bronzing and Galvanizing Works, and thought that the fumes from the bronzing did not agree with me. I fell away to a shadow, as no food that I ate seemed to digest. •

" Getting weaker and weaker, I gave up my employ- ment and got another place, but was no better for the ehinge, and one night, in the spring of 1886, I went horhe more dead than alive, and mothorsaid she thought I would drop dead on the floor. From that time until November, 1889, I !fever knew what it was to be free from pain and suffering. I went tobed tired and got up tired, and it was the same all eday long. I was that

drowsy I could sleep all day and all night, but was not a bit refreshed by it. So heavy and stupid my sleep was that my mother said if a drum was beat at my side, it would not wake me. Last autumn, I got so weak I could do no more than crawl about like an animal that is hurt, and I thought all was about over with me. My father went off in the same way. Mother was nearly heart-broken about me, and had given up all hope, when, one day, in November, 1889, I read in the "Catholic Times" of the wonderful dire of a railway guard by a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. "I read the story to mother, and we were anxious to try the remedy, though we had small hopes of its cur- ing one in my condition. We had lost so much work, and spent so much for medicines, that we could hardly afford the money to buy the Syrup. But mother said, David, you shall give this a trial,' and she parted with her last shilling,, for a bottle, which she bought of Mr: Clelland, the chemist, in Argyle-st. "After the first few doses I got a little better, and after persevering with it a few' weeks, I gradually got stronger, and went back to my work. "You must not imagine I got well all at once, for having been ill all my life it was impossible. But I soon began to eat better. All I took did me good; I slept like other people; the night sweats grew less; and, after tak- ing six bottles, I was healthpand strong for the first ,time since I was born into the world. It,is only fair to say I owe my life to Mother Seigel's Syrup." t Our informant speaks of Mrs. McPhee as a fine-looking lady, and of David as a bonnie lad, who appears more like an educated clerkthan a worker among machinery. David's ailment was profound and chronic indigestion and dyspepsia. We extend our congratulations to his mother and himself, and earnestly hope they will from this time on enjoy health, happinessZand prosperity.

Alaric Orsa has fallen upon the ice, and hurt him- self severely, and upon being informed that you were near by with a sledge, he asked that you might be sent for.' "Been hurt, has he?" "Yes, sir." "Badly ?" "I believe no bones are broken, but he is so badly sprained that he cannot walk." " Ah—then perhaps be wants me to carry him home." "I can't say as to that sir. They only sent me to find you. I don't know the man myself." There was something so frank in the statement thus made that Ruric believed it all honest, and he stood no longer in doubt. "I will go," he said, "but lead the way quickly, for I have no time to waste." "I will lead as fast as you will want to follow," answered the man. And thus speaking he turned back, and having gone some dozen rods by the way they had both come, he turned down a narrow street which led towards the river. Half-way down this he went, and then he turned again—this time to the left— and thus Runic found himself in a narrow, -dark lane, within which the snow was deep and almost untrodden. " Look ye," cried the youth, stopping ashe found himself over knees in snow, "I think we have gone about far enough in this direction." "This is the shortest way," said the stranger guide, apologetically. "I did not think the snow was so deep here. But it's only in the next street.' "Then on you go." Again the stranger started, and Ruric followed on. The lane was a crooked one, and more than once the youth had another inclination to stop. He bad no direct fear, but yet he had some just grounds by doubt. Had he not seen what had been attempted against the ,count, he might have had no such doubts now; but as it was, he thought that if one attempt had been made to ruin him through the Emperor's displeasure by the man who was now try- ing to murder the count, it would not be at all im- probable that some more effective plan should be adopted towards him. He was pondering thus when they came to a cross lane, full as narrow as this, into which the guide turned. "Look ye once more, sirrah," cried the youth, now stopping short. "Do you call this a street ?" "Yes, sir; and on this street we shall find the man we seek. It is only a short cut from where he is to the where your horse is; so you won't have to retrace these dubious ways. Only a little further, sir."

"But I don't like this." "Why—bless you, sir; if you wish to go direct to the inn where your horse is, this will he the nearest way." "Well—on you go." And on they went again—now slipping on the ice—now in the snow to their knees—and anon stumbling along over frozen hubbies and deep holes. At length the guide stopped and opened a small gate which was fixed in a high, thick brick wall. Ituric hesitated here again. He had no weapon of any kind. If he had had even a pistol, or a sword, he would have cared not. But he did not show his thoughts to his guide. The gate opened with a creak upon its frosty hinges, and by the dim star- light the youth could see an open court beyond, and further still, a house of some kind loomed up. "This place seems not to be used much," re- marked Runic; as he saw the snow in the court was trodden but little—only one or two tracks being visible from the.gate to the house." " Ah—yes--you said—what ?" "I said this place didn't seem to be used much," the youth repeated, though he was sure the fellow heard the first time. " Ah, yes—a—the usual entrance is the other way, by the sledge path." And where is it ?" Runic asked, not being able. to see any such path. "Oh—it's around on the other side.' By this time they had reached the door of the house, which our hero could now see had an old dilapidated appearance, and the guide plied the iron knocker with zeal. Ere long a man made his appearance with a lantern in his nand. " All—has the gun-maker come ? the latter asked "Yes," returned the guide. "Well—l'm glad he's here, but I don't believe Ores is fit to move," said the first speaker. And then turning to Runic be said : "But I'm glad you've come, sir, for the lieutenant wishes to see you very much. This way, sir. This was all so frank and prompt that the young man began to think he had been a fool for being frightened. He followed the man with the lantern into the hall, and from thence down a long flight of stairs into a basement. The lantern did not give much light, but it was sufficient to reveal the fact that the house was an old one, and not very large, for Runic could see windows upon the opposite side of the ball which looked out of doors. As he reached the foot or the stairs he found himself upon a brick floor, alid he saw that the walls were of stone. A little further on a door was opened, and this led to a small apartment within which was a fireplace, and a good fire burning. "There, good sir," said the second guide, "if you will wait a few moments I will go and see how the lieutenant is." As soon as Ituric was left alone he looked about him. The room was of moderate size for a small house, and the idea of inhabiting the cellars was a common one in Moscow during the winter season. The windows, two in number, were close up to the ceiling, and very small, and were patched with pieces of board in two or three places. Ere long the man came back, and with him came three others, one of whom the youth recognized as the individual who had conducted him to the house. " Orsa will see you, sir," said he with the lantern. Runic arose to follow him, the other three men approaching the fire as though they would remain there. He had reached the door and passed through into the room beyond, when he thought he heard footsteps behind 13inl. It was a sliding, shuffling sound, and he turned his head to see what it was. As he did so he reeeived a blow which staggered him, and which would have felled an ordinary man to the floor. Ile gathered himself quickly up, but before he could fairly turn about he received a second blow, heavier than the first, which brought him upon his knees. In an instant all four of the men were upon him, and he could see that they had ropes in their hands with which to bind him. With all his might he threw the fellow who held his right hand back against the wall, and another he sent in an opposite direction, and in a moment more he rould have been upon his feet; but just at that in- Stant a noose was adroitly slipped over his head, and as the rope tightened about his neck he was drawn back upon the brick floor again. “Now resist any more, and we'll choke you as sure as fate," cried the man who had held the lantern, and who now had a hold upon the rope. "Oh groaned Runic, while the massive cords worked like cables in his arms and shoulders, " give me a fair chance. Let me be up and free—then lock your doors, if you please." "No, no, good sir," replied the ruffian, with a wicked smile. "We know your power, and we are not disposed to test it further. We have had trouble enough *already. Shall we—" The man stopped speaking, for at that moment another noose was slipped down over Ruric's heady and ere he could avoid it, it had been drawn tightly about his arms. He was now at the mercy of his captors, and having rolled him over upon his breast they proceeded to secure his arms behind him, which being done they bade him to rise. Of course he could have no desire to lie there upon the cold bricks, and he got upon his feet as well as he could. "Now, Runic Novel, I will conduct you to your own apartment," said the leader of the gang. " But wherefore is this? "the gun-maker gasped. rendered almost speechless with the mingled emo- tions of surprise and anger. "Why have ye done this? Whose hirelings are ye that ye thus waylay and seize upon an honest man who has done no harm to any of you ? " "Never mind that now, sir," the ruffian 'coolly answered, "suffice it for you to know that you are safe for the present." • "But will ye not tell me what this is for? There is some intent." "Yes—and come with me and you shall see. Come." Thus speaking the man turned once more, and having picked up his lantern he moved on, while the others, taking Runic by the arms, followed after. The prisoner made no resistance now, for be knew that it would be useless. At a short distance another flight of stairs was reached. "Down here?" uttered Runic, with a shudder. "Of course. You'd freeze up here." These words struck harshly upon the youth's soul, for it meant that he was to be detained in this lonesome place. At the bottom of these stairs they came to a vaulted passage, at the end of which was 'a door. This was opened, and Runic was led through into the place beyond, He cast his eyes quickly about,
FUNERAL OF UTE ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.

On Tuesday, the remains of Dr. Thomson, Archbishop of York, were committed to their last resting place. Al- though it was felt that York Minster would be an appro- priate place of sepulture, yet, in compliance with the deceased prelate's last wish, the funeral—which was of a quiet and unostentatious character—took place in the local churchyard adjoining the Palace of Bishopthorpe. A commemorative service was first held in the Minster, at which there were present the Archbishop of Canter- bury, and the Bishops of Durham, Winchester, New- castle, Ripon, Wakefield, Sordor and Man, Beverley, and Richmond. The officiating clergy were the Bishop Suf- fragan of Beverley and the Dean of York, assisted by the Archdeacons of the diocese, and the Rev. R. Blakeneyt vicar of Bishopthorpe.

div.head: AN ARMY ROMANOE.
div.p: AN ARMY ROMANOE.

In Vienna (says a Correspondent) there may be ob- served any day walking on the Ringstrasse arm-in-arm a very handsome woman of twenty dressed in the height of fashion, and a common soldier, in the uniform of the Vienna regiment called " Deutschmeister." They are husband and wife. Twelve years ago the young man's father, a wealthy suburban manufacturer, was made to believe that with one hundred pounds he could free his son from military service. He paid, and the youth re- ceived a document upon which was written "Examined and found unfit." After receiving this document, he was twice married, his first wife dying a few months after the marriage. When he went to get a passport for his second honeymoon, which he wished to spend in England, the Police Commissioner expressed surprise that he should have been found unfit for military service, and when the young man frankly said that he had been freed from military duty by means of a thousand florins the affair was looked into. The official who twelve years ago took the bribe died by his own hand a short time ago. In the military archives the young man's name was found with the remark, "Died in childhood." As the authorities were convinced that the manufacturer and his son were both dupes and never meant to commit a fraud, no punishment was given, but the young millionaire of thirty-two, with a handsome establishment and a beano.- ' ful wife, has to do his three sears' service in the bar racks of the "loch mid Deutschmeisters."

div.head: MONEY-MAKERS' WILLS,
div.p: MONEY-MAKERS' WILLS,

As affording confirmation of the wholesome fact that it is industry and commerce, and not mere speculative ingenuity,which help to swell the cata- logue of fortune makers, some twenty wills are re- ported during the year from the North of England alone which each represent personality over --C400,000. Oddly enough, however, it is a solicitor-- Mr. John Clayton,of New-castle-on-Tyne--who heads the score. He was for many years Town Clerk /0 that great human hive, and died at the great age of ninety-eight, leaving behind him £728,746—or cousiderably more than two million eix and eight peaces. The Newcastle folk are presumptively fond of law. Perhaps the best known of the twenty 15 the late Mr. Thomas Andrew Walker, contractor for the Severn Tunnel and the Manchester SW Canal, who died at the comparatively early age of sixty-one, leaving considerably over half-a, million. Besides these, thenorthern countries yiele eighteen whose personalty, though under .C 400,064 was still above half that sum. They figured under the various descriptions of cotton spinner, engineer, merchant, sugar refiner, hide broker, linen manll; facturer, and distiller; and included, in the ease 0' Mr. Nasmyth, the inventor of the steam hammer, at least one name of world-wide renown. Among the curiosities of reoent will-making is the bequ.ol! of the late Mr: John Noble, the millionaire varniall manufacturer, of an annual income to his son. gr' Wilson Noble, the present member fcr Hastings, with the proviso that .C 2,000 a-year shad at once 0,5 struck off if he should fail to be re-elected. " TI,S not," as Mr. Addison has reminded us, "in mortals to command success," though they may de.srCe it ;" and Mr. Noble, even under the prop!tiou? political skies If 1886, only out-stripped the Liberal candidate by some 335 votes in a total poll of nearq five thousand. But though the extra £2,000 a-yeg is to be lost if he loses his seat, it is to come back to him again if he can find a seat anywhere.

MR. PARNELL AND MR. O'BRIEN AT BOULOGNE.

BOOLOGNE-SUR-MER, DECEMBER 30.—Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Gill, leaving Amiens shortly after midday, arrived here almost simultaneously with Mr. Parnell and his friends, who came from London by the Folkestone route. The member for Cork was accompanied by Mr. • John Redmond, M.P., Mr. Wm. Redmond, M P., Dr. Kenny, M.P. Mr. Clancy, M.P., Mr. Vincent Scully, and Dr. Byrne, of "The Freeman's Journal." The entire party on disembarking at once proceeded to the Hotel du Louvre, whither they had already been preceded by Mr. W. O'Brien and Mr. Gill. The latter gentleman was the first to meet Mr. Parnell, who appeared in good health, notwithstanding the bandage which he still wears over his eyes. The valious members having ex- changed greetings, those between Mr. Parnell and Mr. W. O'Brien being marked by great cordiality, the mem- ber for Cork and Mr. O'Brien entered a private sitting • room, previously engaged by telegraph, where they had about half-an-hour's conversation. The other gentlemen then came in, and shortly afterwards all the members and their friends lunched together. It was expected this evening that Mr. Parnell would leave here shortly after midnight for Calais, en route for London,but at a late hour to-mghtit was announced that this arrangement had been altered. The following com- munication respecting the negotiations has just been issued by the Irish members: "Mr. Yarnell and Mr. O'Brien met here to-day and had a prolonged conversation, which will be resumed in a few days." AMIENS, DEC. 30.—Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Gill passed the night in this city. At ten o'clock this morning they did not know whether it would be necessary for them to go to Boulogne or wait here. Subsequently however they received a telegram, in consequence of which they determined to start by the midday train for Boulogne- sur-Mer. PROBABLE TERMS OF COMPROMISE. Bouts:x:4)m, WEDNDSDAY AFTERNOON.—Further ex- changes of opinion took place last evening between Messrs. O'Brien and Parnell and other members of the two sections. As far as can be ascertained, no actual agreement has been arrived at. I have reason to be- lieve that a compromise was proposed, and received not • altogether unfavourably by the Parnellites, upon the basis that Mr. Parnell shall retire after designating Mr. O'Brien as his successor as chairman of the 'Parliamen- tary party. None of the hon. gentlemen here will con- firm or deny this version of the negotiations. Shortly after three o'clock Mr. O'Brien received me in No. 4 sitting room at the Hotel du Louvre, Mr. Gill also being present. The latter said he could say nothing more than that a conference had been held and would be re- sumed. Mr. Parnell left with Dr. Kenny and several other friends by the afternoon steamer, Folkestone, en route for London.

MR. PE.RNELL IN LONDON. Mr. Parnell, accompanied by. Dr. Kenny, M.P., Mr. Vincent Scully, and Dr. Byrne arrived at Charing-cross at six o'clock on Wednesday night. In reply to a repre- sentative of the Press who saw Mr. Parnell on his arrival, the member of Cork said he was quitehimself again. The condition of his eye was so much improved that he was able to dispense with the bandage, and, in fact, he was better in health than he had been for some time. Mr. Parnell returns at once to Ireland, but he will not resume his campaign for the present. MR. O'BRIEN AND HIS SENTENCE. The "Dublin Express" states that, according to a private telegram, it is the intention of Mr. William O'Brien to give himself up to the police at Dover early in January. THREATENED REVELATIONS. Canon O'Mahony, Adm. Cork Cathedral, addressing a meeting of the Cork "National Committee," said it was stated on Parnell platforms that since the Leinster Hall meeting nothing had occurred except Mr. Gladstone's letter which would be a reason for Mr. Parnell's deposi- tion. That was not the fact. Something had occurred which was sufficient to alienate any honest and self- respecting member of Parliament from Mr. Parnell. Mr. Parnell had made a certain revelation to the Irish mem- bers intended to exculpate himself from what had occurred. That revelation was not to be published, and the members of the party who were opposed to him had under circumstances of great pthvocation extended to Mr. Parnell the charity of silence. Mr. Parnell's action since had been such that he (Canon O'Mahony) con- sidered these members would be perfectly justified in making this matter public, and show the sort of man Mr. Parnell was. It would horrify the public far more than the proceedings in the divorce court. If they did not do so, and if the Parnell propaganda continued, he (Canon O'Mahony) would take it upon himself to make the matter public. MR. PARNELL AND MRS. O'SFIEA. The " Insuppressible " of Wednesday evening, in the course of an article on the Parnell-O Shea affair, says Mr. Parnell wants no" vindication" which would lead to the undoing of the divorce, assigning as a reason that he intends to marry Mrs. O'Shea, and that under the compromise effected regarding the probate' suit she will receive £50,000 instead of the £190,000 bequeathed her by Mrs. Wood, of Eltham. The " Insuppressible " goes on to say that it has for some time been in posses- sion of copies of telegrams sent daily from Mr. Parnell to Mrs. O'Shea, telling her not to be alarmed by the accounts of the lime throwing incident purveyed for public consumption. SUGGESTED RESIGNATION OF MR. PARNELL. PARIS, THURSDAY.—There is the very best authority for stating that at the conference al Boulogne Mr. Par- nell, in order to remove the deadlock and the contest between the Irish factions, expressed his willingness to retire if Mr. Wm. O'Brien were appointed chairman. There is equally good reason for the assertion that in- formation to this effect was yesterday cabled to Mr. Dillon in America. MRS. O'SHEA'S PROBATE SUIT.

The Press Association says thete is no foundation for the report that Mrs. O'Shea has compromised the probate suit instituted against her by her brother, Sir Evelyn Wood and others, by accepting £50,000 in lieu of the £1.90,000 devised to her under the will of her aunt, Mrs. Wood, of Eltham. The probate suit, which has been Pending for the past year, will, it is expected, come on Shortly after Easter, and the preparations for the bear- ing of the action are now in full progress. Sir Evelyn Wood and others who were beneficiaries under form cr Wills complain of the omission of their names from the final one. There is no truth in the allegation that the will of Mrs.. Wood was drawn up or witnessed by Mr: Parnell, the document having been preilared by Mrs. Wood's solicitor and witnessed by him and his managing clerk.

The Press Association says that a communication as received in London on Thursday from. Mr. William O'Brien,' M.P., expressing a belief that the result of the coerence at' Boulogne would be an amicable arrange- 'net of the differences at present existing among the Nationalist members of Parliament.

MR. GLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.

MESSAGES OF CONGRATULATION. Mr. Gladstone celebrated his 81st birthday on Mon- day, with his family surrounding him, at Hawarden Castle. It has been the custom for some years now to shower congratulations on the right hon. gentleman on these anniversaries, and there was no exception to the rule on Monday. The Post Office was almost monopolised, indeed, by the business of Hawarden Castle. Beginning the day with a phenomenal letter bag, Mr. Gladstone was well-nigh incessantly engaged for hour after hour in receiving messages or gifts. Some of the latter were very curious. One gentleman. who had, perhaps, some knowledge of the way in which the ex-Premier exposes himself at public functions, sent him a hat, in the hope that he would wear it. Another went to the opposite extreme, and sent him a pair of socks, while a third, a boy of 14, sent him a sketch of his own portrait. The messages were more remarkable still. One advised Mr. Gladstone to " stick to Paddy ; " and quite a number referred him to texts in the Bible. From Silsden, the ex-Premier was told that the cause sf Home Rule for Ireland has "passed through a filtering bed," and from Dalkeith, that "Mr. Parnell's retirement is imperatively demanded by recent events." "Warrington friends sent warmest congratulations, and added: "May God preserve your health for many years." Many of the messages were in Welsh; one, at least, was in German; and still another was in Greek. Royalty was represented in the messages by the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Princess Louise, and the late Cabinet by Lord Rose- bery, Sir Wm. Harcourt. and Mr. John Mdrley.• Cardinal Manning, too, wired congratulations, as did also a great many other public personages. No fewer than 1,400 letters and telegrams of congratu- lation were received, During the afternoon a handsome drinking fountain, which the people of Hawarden have erected in the village in commemoration of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone's golden wedding, was unveiled by Mrs. Johnson, a lady residing in the neighbourhood. It is the work of Mr. Edward Griffith, sculptor, of Chester. The structure, which is of solid masonry, is of an imposing character, the dimensions of which reveal the fact that several of .the large blocks of stone average two tons each in weight. The plan of the fountain,is circular, the diameter being lift. 6in., occupying a position in the centre of the vil- lage, at the junction of the Chester, Wrexham, and Con- nah's Quay roads. The fountain from itebaseinent is up- wards of 21ft. in height. The work throughout carries with it its full meaning, which is at one apparent to the observer, the whole being studiously designed, bearing with it the impress of a marriage gift, carrying to the finish the attributes of Hymen, "The god of marriage." Mr. Gladstone in acknowledging the presentation spoke of the comfort which such means of refreshment afforded to the population. He trusted that though returns of that day could not be many, yet they might find him engaged in his best efforts for the performance of duty, and in close, constant, unvarying, and affectionate attachment to his Hawarden neighbours, At the con- clusion of the speech, a respectably-dressed woman pressed forward and seizing the distinguished statesman by the hand kissed it fervently, adding, "I'm Irish ; God bless you." On Monday evening, Liberals in various towns in the Kingdom celebrated the birthday by meetings, tea- parties, and dinners.

div.head: GLADSTONE BIRTHDAY SOIREE AT
div.p: GLADSTONE BIRTHDAY SOIREE AT
RUNCORN. SPEECHES BY MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND OTHERS.

In celebration of Mr. Gladstone's 81st birthday, a soiree was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Mon- day night, in connection with Runcorn Liberal Club. The proceedings aimmenced at seven o'clock, with a tea, provided in capital style by Messrs. Spearing. of Church-st. Afterwards a concert was held under the presidency of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who forwarded a telegram to Mr. Gladstone in the following terms : Runcorn Liberal Club sends hearty congratulations and expresses una- bated confidence in your leadership.' The first item on the programme was the appropriate song, "Our Leader,' written by Mr. W. Handley, secre- tary to the party, Mr: F. Scott rendering it in capi- tal style. A topical song, " Hear, Hear,"' also writtenby Mr. Handley, and sung by Mr. Scott was highly amusing and Mr. Scott had to respond to a votiferous recall. The other items on the pro- gramme were the duet, "The minute gun at sea," sung by Messrs. Morris and Leathwood and the song," Will o' the Wisp," by Mr. T. Clegg. Mr. E. W. Humphreys, and Mr. R. Musgrave were the accompanists. In the course of the evening speeches .were delivered as under : The Chairman said they had not come to listen to long speeches, but had gathered together in a social way to look into each others faces on the day they all thought one of the brightest days in the year—the birthday of their great leader. (Applause.) He was therefore, not going to occupy very much time. It was nevertheless, a duty en the part of every public man at this juncture, to declare his opinion with regard to the Irish question, In view of what the speaker last Saturday called "the traitor's fall." (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Brunner) had never for one moment abated his hope that the Grand Old Man would pass a measure of Home Rule. (Ap- plause.) The fact that there had been a traitor amongst the Irish Parliamentary party, Was not one that ought to deter the Liberal party—they had had their traitors. Just as they had lost Mr. Chamberlain and recovered from the loss entirely, so, he believed the Irish Parlia- mentary party would recover from the loss of Mr. Parnell (Applause.) Mr. Brave Balfour had lately not shown quite as much courage as usual. It was a remarkable factlhat Mr. Harrison, one of the latest recruits, who had a warrant out against him, was allowed to go free because he was a supporter of Mr. Parnell, and because it was known that Mr. John Morley was to visit Ireland and to give evidence. These weneto him very encourag- ing signs, and they ought to determine the Liberal party not to abate their efforts for a moment. They had only got to show their courage, and Mr. Balfour would show a similar want .of 'courage to that which he had displayed recently. Their efforts were to be directed not only to passing a Measure of Home Rule, but to the removal of the standing dis- grace uptm the English name—they had to get rid of this abominable system of coercion in Ireland. (Ap- plause.) The question was when were we going to have a General Election. For his part he believed that Mr. Gladstone bad so endeared himself to all right thinking men and wemen in England by his action in 'writing that celebrated letter to Mr. Morley, and that the feeling I of justice of the people was outraged by the threat to imprison Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon, and that come ! when an election may, the Liberal party would sweep the country. (Applause.) He noticed that they in i Runcorn had now an opportunity of taking advantage of the Technical Instruction Act' 1889. • (Hear, hear.) He did not say, as some did, that they had done enough , far the working classses. They had spent a great deal of money for their benefit since 1870, but he wished they had spent three times, or four times as much. (Hear, hear.) He believed that it would have been thoroughly wise and economic expenditure, but surely it was time that the trading class and the professional clags should ' 'get some benefit from the expenditure of the State and I here was an opportunity. They in Runcorn taxed them- • selves about 3d. in the £ for the education of the children ;of the working Classes., and would not grudgea penny for the children of 'tradesmen 'and the children of profes- sional men. He trusted -that they would encourage those in whose hands this matter lay, at their •coming meeting, and that they would strengthen their hands and declare each and all of them that the expenditure of id. under the Technical Instruction Act, wilt be the wisest step that ever the Board of Commissioners had taken. (Hear, hear.) He declared hiinself in favour of Free Education, and scouted the idea that it would pauperise the people, and he could not understand how reasonable men could repeat such utter nonsense. (Applatise.). He had had pleasure in sending in the name 'of' the club, their hearty congratulations and good wishes to their great leader. (Applause.) He wished he could use the eloquent .Words which Mr. Chamberlain used in speaking of Mr. Gladstone a few years ago, and he wished Mr. Chamberlain would repeat them with such 'sincerity as he showed on that occasion. (Hear, hear.) But though he could not use such eloquence he could speak from the bottom of his heart and express the hope that Mr. Glad- stone would live to complete his work, and that God would bless him and his family. (Applause.) ' Mr. A. R. Norman chairman of the Committee of the Club, said this was the second time they had celebrated Mr. Gladstone's birthday in connection with the club and he hoped it would become an annual institution; and that Mr. Gladstone would live long and enable them to hold the gathering. (Applause.) After referring to 'their club he expressed his pleasure that Mr. Brunner, their president was in the chair. They were very much obliged to him for coming on such a night at consider- able personal inconvenience. (Applause.) Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys said if they could not con- gratulate themselves upon the numbers that were present, he hoped they would make up for that by their enthusiasm. It appeared to him that if ever they were under a debt of gratitude to their great leader it was at the present time—(applause)—for the noble letter to which their worthy president had referred. His courage no less than his fidelity to principle had raised the Liberal party to a pitch which was utterly unex- pected, and which reflected the greatest credit upon it, supposing he represented the opinions of the party at large. (Applause.) He felt that they ,were met that evening under the best auspices. There was a time immediately 4fter the unfortunate difficulty with Mr. Parnell, when it was felt that the Liberal party had sustained an irretrievable blow; but North Kilkenny had done wonders in raising their spirits. We were essentially —or professed to be—a Christian country and at this solemn time of the year, and in the light of those great principles, which in words they had upon their lips, ask themselves and decide which of the two policies— coercion or conciliation—was most likely to produce on earth peace and good will towards men. (Applause.) Mr. .1. J. Howett said he was very glad that Mr. Branner had stood tohi° ""'" '1 our present position.

(Applause.) Shakespeare could not write the characters of the Romans, in their time the most literary and elo- quent people without he found an lago amongst them; in the twelve,diciples there was a Judas Iscariot ; and it would have been marvellous if the Liberal party had not had a Parnell. But that did not in the least injure the cause. He was happy to say that although they had had a Cave of Abdullam amongst the Liberals they were still on the right side of.victory which would no doubt be achieved by and bye by their great leader. (Applause.) If there was anything in the character of Englishmen that stood out more than anything else it was their love of virtue and honour, and when Mr. Gladstone pub- lished his letter to Mr. Morley it proved that he was a true and noble Egglishman besides being one of thegreat- est politicians this country had ever seen. (Applause.) Mr. E. Marshall remarked that Mr. Gladstone must have been in terrible trouble during the past fortnight, and he was sure that the telegram sent from that hall and from numerous others would put heart into the old man. (Hear, hear.) He claimed that the Irish people by their sound decision in North Kilkenny had shown their aptitude for self-government and he urged them in North- wich division to send Mr. Brunner back to Parliament at the next election with a mandate to free Ireland from the thraldom of coercion and give her self-government because they were anxious not only to do what was right but to clear the line for their own legislative proposals. (Applause.) Mr. Jepson also delivered a speech in which he said no statesman had done so much for the working classes. Mr. T. Clegg proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Brunner for his kindness in taking the chair at great personal sacrifice.—Mr. W. Handley seconded the motion which was carried enthusiastically. Mr. Brunner briefly responded, and then the room was cleared for dancing. Mr. J. Ravenscroft was at the piano and Mr. Spearing provided the refreshments.
TOTAL ABSTINEDrCE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.

During the week the Warrington Workingmen's Open-air Total Abstinence Mission have celebrated their first anniversary by holding a tea party and several meetings. On Sunday afternoon a meeting; was held in the 03-operative Hall, Sankey-st., pre- sided over by Councillor H. Roberts. Amongst others present were the Rev. T. Ross and Councillor Dixon.—The CHAIRMAN, in the course of an open- ing address, said that he did not think it would be right to allow that opportunity to pass without congratulating the mission on reaching its first anniversary. When working-meii listened to those of their own rankin life they were far more likely to be impressed by what they heard, because they knew that such men had been through the same temptations as themselves. The thought that was constantly occurring to his mind was that Warring- ton had unfortunately got the name of rather a drunken town, and it was prefectly true that they were unfortunately rather worse than some towns in that respect. There were apprehended in War- rington every year something like 700 people for being drunk, and some of them for being also disor- derly. Some were fined and some were sent to pri- son, and yet every year, although these people had been made drunk somewhere, these were only taken to the bridewell for consideration by the magistrates the cases of some four or five publicans who had made them drunk. These men and women who were apprehended were not made drunk in the street, and it was a shame and a disgrace to the town that such acondition cf things should exist. It was an offence against the law to serve a man already in a condition of intoxication, and yet I they saw such men rolling out of public houses day after day. Who should lotik after this matter? They put men in a position to employ proper officials for this purpose, land they had a right to know how it was that this thing was allowed. It was an offence against the law that children of tender years should bs served over a publi- can's counter, but he ventured to say that there was no one in that room but had frequently seen little ones come out of public houses with bottles. They knew that an offence had been committed in the serving of that drink, bat still the offence was going on. They them- selves were responsible. As long as they remained dumb and allowed these things to go on they were responsible for the maintenance of the present disgraceful condition of things. They had it in their power to ventilate public opinion on this question, and if they did so the present condition of things would cease Even ths corporation of Warrington would shrink in time to come from the pressure of public opinion, and from the dis- credit of putting upon the watch committee publicans and brewers, and at the same time refus- ing a seat upon that committee to men who happened to be teetotallers.—An address was also I given by Mr. J. H. WARLOW who dealt mainly with his I own experiences in regard to the effects of intoxicating; drinks.—A third speaker was the Rev. T. Ross who com- plimented the Chairman upon hisstraightforward way of speaking out upon the drink question in Warrington. He also referred to the fact that the clergy of Liverpool had banded themselves together and had sent word to the Watch Committee that they would do all in their power to help it in carrying out the law of the land. He was of opinion that in a town like Warrington the law ought to be thoroughly put into force. It was a burning shame that so few publicans should be caught for serving drunken men with drink. (Applause.) During the meet ing Sankey's hymns were sung, and at its close a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman and other speakers, SUNDAY EVENING. A meeting was held in the evening, over which Mr. Councillor J. Shaw Green presided. He was supported on the platform by the Rev. John Davies, Mr. John Walker, Mr. J. Price, president, Mr. Robertson, secre- tary, Mr. Pemberton, Mr. J. Gandy, and Mr. J. H. Warlow.—The Chairman in his opening speech expressed the opinion that outdoor missionizing was the best way of reaching the masses, who felt that beautiful places of worship were not for them to enter. He commented on the advance which the temperance movement had made since the days when nothing savouring of total abstin- tence was tolerated from the pulpit. He thanked God that there had been a dovetailing, merging, and joining ogether of Christianity and total abstinence, and under the two they had one grand and glorious movement which he believed would some time reclaim the country. —Mr. Walker next addressed the meeting. In the course of his remarks he said he had seen some little of Lanca- shire towns, and he was convinced, from observation, that Warrington was one of the most drink-ridden towns in the county ; and that from a study of statistics there was more,drunkenness amongst women than there was in any other town of its size in the kingdom. After giving a number of quotations from -Shakespeare against drinkitig, and in favour of temperance, he com- mented on the advanze the temperance cause was making in public opinion, as proved by the determined opposition to the Compensation Bill, and proceeded In answer to the argument against prohibition to adduce the case of Texteth, (Liver- pool), where public-houses were prohibited, with the result that the rates, instead of being 2s. 6d. to 3s. in the £,• as was formerly the case had been brought down to ls. and even 10d. in the £, saving the ratepayers £20,000 to £30,000' a year.—The Rev. J. Davies foliowed. He said he had been simply amazed at the amount of drunkenness in Warrington, and he quoted an opinion published' in a Welsh magazine in 1832, classing Warring- ton as the worst place in England in point of drinking. • Referring to General Booth's work he expressed the opinion that nine-tenths of the misery of" Darkest Eng- land" was-clue to drink. Diink, he pointed out, would weaken herediarily the will pbwer oft coming generations to resist it. Madnets was being increased by it; 69 per cent. of the lin:lack' of Scotland being' now due to it as compared with 47 per cent., 10 years ago—Mr. Drury moved, Mr. Warlovrseconded, and Mr. Price supported a vote of thanks to the Chairman, the other speakers, and the pianist, Miss Pemberton, who had accompanied hymns sung during the evening, also solos by Mr., Mar- shall. The vote was carried with hearty acclamatibn. THE TEA MEETING. On Monday evening the first annual soirée in connet:. tion with the mission was held in the Co-operative Hall. About 140 persons partook of tea, which was followed by an excellent entertainment, interspersed with addresses. There was a large attendance. The Rev. F. W. Willis presided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. J. Yonge and Thomas Ross, Mr. G. Drury, Mr. J. Ince (president), Mr. E. Robertson (secretary), and Mr. J. H. Warlow. A pianoforte solo having .been given by Miss Pemberton, the Chairman delivered an address. He said though not a total abstainer, he was stronely in favour of temperance ; and where necessary,of total abstinence. He also took great interest in that mission, because it

SANGUINARY ENCOUNTER. 300 REDSKINS KILLED. Omaha and Bismarck telegrams report a terrific en- counter between United States troops and the hostile Indians entrenched in the Badlands. Sec:nits had for some days been aware of the whereabouts of the Indian encampment, and during Sunday night five hundred United States soldiers drew a cordon round it. WOUNDED KNEE CREEK, (NEBRASKA,) DEC. 29.—The troops were in readiness at eight o'clock in the morning, when the cavalry were dismounted and the men massed about the Indian village with Hotchkiss guns in position overlooking the camp, which was not fifty yards distant. Colonel Forsythe then ordered the Indians to come for- ward from their tents, upon which the braves advanced and sat in a semicircle until they had been counted. The dismounted troops then surrounded them in companies under the commands of Captains Wallace and Varnum, and the order was given for twenty Indians to get their guns. Upon their return, however, it was seen that only two guns had been brought, and a detachment began to search the village, with the result that 38 guns were found. The order was then given for the warriors to be searched, and while this was going on the Indians, who were surrounded by the troops, began to move. They suddenly drew rifles from under their blankets and commenced firing rapidly, the troops at the time not being twenty feet distant, and at a disadvantage, as they feared shooting their com- rades. The Indians ran in a southerly direction, pur- sued by the cavalry, who shot them on every side. The engagement lasted an hour and a half. Many of the braves sought refuge in a ravine, where it is difficult to dislodge them. Over fifty Indians were killed outright. The soldiers shot the Indians wherever they found them, giving no quarter. The troops are still firing upon camp, and are pursuing the enemy in every direction. It was a daring feat for 120 Indians to attack a body of cavalry 500 strong, and it is doubtful whether at nightfall there will be either a buck or a squaw out of all Big Foot's band left. There were many single hand-to-hand con- flicts during the night. Captain Wallace was killed by a blow on the head from a war club. NEW Yoax, DEC. 30.—A telegram to the "Herald," from Pine Ridge states that in the fighting at Porcupine Creek seventy-five of the American cavalrymen were killed and wounded, while on the Indian side one hun- dren and ten warriors and two hundred and fifty omen and children were killed. The telegram adds, that of the. whole Indian:camp probably not more than six chil- dren remain alive. . . . .

The Indian agent at Pine Ridge telegraphs that three hundred Indians, including women and children were killed in the engagement at Porcupine Creek. Wenn/gavot.; Jsc 29.—Referring to the fighting at Porcupine Creek, General Schofield said, that whilst regretting the occurrence, be was not surprisedat Indian treachery. ge did not think that there was any further danger, except that from the disarming of bands still out, although it Was possible that the excitement follow- ing Monday's fight might lead to further trouble. Mr. Proctor, Setretary for War, has expressed the opinion that, inasmuch as Big Foot was connected with Sitting /Bull's band, the attack was a CBSe :of revenge. MORE FIGHTING.

News was received at _Pine Ridge, on Wednesday, that six men of the 7th cavalry Regiment had been killed and many woundiadih the encounter with the in- dians who had surrounded and fired the Clay Creek Mission Station. The lodians are supposed to be the same who escaped from the Agency upon heating of the defeat at Wounded Knee Creek. The fire after*ards proved to be confined to the day school of the mission. -
