• GHOST STORY.

Was I ever married? No, ma'am; never. I've lived a single life for sixty years,_ and I've been the ferryman for forty: There'll be a steamer here next year, they say, and then maybe my work is done. I've enough to live on, though, and it's not all f',r the bit of pay that I row the boat. I've had all these long years that would have made ionic; folk fear to let me row them over the ferry, but I think I'll tell you all about it, for you've a look in your eyes as though you could understand. When I was twenty I had a sweetheart. Her name was Jessie. We had been betrothed a wee while, and the banns were to be put up in the *kirk in a month's time, when suddenly her mother took a dislike to me, and said it should not be. It was only an old woman's freak. An ill-tempered body she was, and not quite right in her mind, I think. But Jessie would not marry against her mother's will. She cried like a baby, and vowed to me to be true, and to meet me every Saturday at least. And she hoped to soften her mother in time. What could I do? Nothing but fret'and fume, and make her unhappier than she was. You know man's nature well enough to know that I did that, I've no doubt, ma'am. But Saturday afternoons I always rowed about the edge of the loch here, waiting for Jessie. She'd come to the bank--I can see her still, in her little straw bonnet, with a pink rose in it—and wave her handkerchief. Then I'd go to her; and we'd row about until sunset, keeping well out of sight, as it was easy to do. Not many people wanted to cross, but if they came at that time they had to go back again. I ' never answered them. And though I worried and fretted enough in all conscience, those were very happy afternoons. We met so for a year. The old mother never grew any more willing that I should court Jessie, and never guessed that she met me on the lake. She wanted Jessie to marry a rich old man, and the poor girl had a hard time of it at home. At last, between them, the old man .always following her about, the mother always pleading his cause, she was half distracted. I urged her to run away with me, and vowed that I could make a fortune in Edinburgh if she was my wife.. And she was almost worn out. And when the old woman declared that she should marry . at Christmas
BOLTON PUBLICANS AND THE NEW
YEAR.

An application was made on Tuesday morning to a Judge in Chambers in London against the decision of the Bolton borough magistrates to grant an extension to pub- licans and beersellers in the town of one hour on New Year's Eve and the evening of Now Year's Day. After hearing the grounds of the appeal of the temperance party as given at the time of the application, through counsel, the Judge made an order 'absolute for certirorai to issue to bring up the order to be quashed. The Judge, however, refused to grant costs. The effect of this de- cision is that the order for extension made on the 22nd inst. is quashed, and until a further application has Peen made by the publicans and 'a new order made by the magistrates there will be no extension. On Wednesday the Bolton justices had under consider- ation the action of the Queen's Bench in quashing their decision. There were nineteen magistrates present, and after a heated deliberation, by eleven votes to eight they re-affirmed their decision to grant the extension.
whether she would or not, she proinised me to leave home.

"It would be a crime to marry Mr. MeGreggor," she said, "with nothine, but dislike to give him; but I fear it is a sin to deceive my mother." Then she wept in my arms and promised to meet me the next Saturday at the same hour and go to Edinburgh with me. I was to take her across the lake, and after that sway townward in the stage coach.
It was hard to wait for Saturday, but it came; everything was ready. I role the boat out upon the lake and sat waiting. .

I waited long. Th; evening was drawing on, and there was no sign of her. I grew anxious. I grew despairing. I could not believe she would willingly break a ron-iise to me. I feared her niSltter haa discovered everything. At last, as the twilight fell and I was in despair, T. saw her standing on the shore. She was dresied all in white, ai jri;bcx hinking that it was not like my sensible Jessie to (teZt. bride for a dusty journey to the dirty town, when we were anxious to hide from any who might follow. But when I had taken the boat across I saw that she had no ha, or parcel with her, that she had not even aha upon her head. What She wore was a sort of robe loosely hanging on her figure, and her feet were barn. "The mother ha S locked her up," I said to myself, "and she's escaped just this way, brave lass." And I took off my plaid and made ready to hap it around her when she got in. When I got close to her so that I could see her face. it was as pale as a lily. I was frightened at it, and I called out: "What have they been doing to you, my lassie ?" She made no answer, but came into my boat. "Don't touch me yet," she said; but she took my plaid and laid it about her, and looked at me sad and strange and woeful. "I said I would come, and. I came," she whispered. "Oh, Jamie, lad, we might have been so happy." "We will," I said. "Come to me, Jessie."

"Oh, Jamie," she said again, "don't touch me yet. Lengthen the moments as long as you can, for when you touch me I must go. I'll be yours in heaven, Jamie, remember that. "But here first, Jessie," I said. "You shall never go back to those who have used you so ill."

"No, I shall never go hick," she said. The voice was not Jessie's, it was so sad and faint. The face was whiter than marble. The eyes seemed to look at me through a mist; and, indeed, a mist was all about her, _
I drew my oars into the boat. "Come close, Jessie," 1 said. me make you warm in my arms." I stretched them out. heshrank away.
"Tell me all. Let

oh, --Jamie, Jamie ! " she sighed, the cold mould must hap me not your arms. Death is my bridegroom. Good:by ! Good-by! ood-by !" I caught her in my arms. It was as if I had plunged into the heart of a cold mist. I saw her, but I could not hold her as she faded away. An hour after, some one found me drifting in the boat. I was out of my head and I as ill a long while. When I came to myself they told me that as I waited for my love in my boat oh the great loch, she lay shrouded in her mother's home. She died suddenly of beart disease after a terrible scene with the old woman.

I've never left the loch since. I've been the ferryman ever since, but it is not for the money. I hope always that sume slay 1 may see Jessie on the bank again, and that, at least, once more her spirit will sail with me ever the blue water— perhaps at the moment when I am ready to go away with her to the heaven where she has been so many years.

"Who i he? " said a parser-by to a policeman who was endeavourin,* to raise an intoxicated in- dividual who had fall'en into the gutter. "9e.n't say, sir," replied the policeman ; "he can't give no account of himself." "Of •course not," said the other ; "how caii you expect an account from a person who has lost his balance ? " A CORRESPONDENT A.SKS : "What time of year do the days begin to shorten ? " When you have a note in bank. A hote in bank is the great annihilator of time. The days are crowded to- gether in thin layers and the nights are like a smear from a blacking brush. IRISH WIT.-Witty things innumerable are told of the Dublin carmen; one is, that on a wet day, driving ai English fare through Ackville-street, as they passed 'the General Post Office, the en- tablature of which is surmounted by three allegorical figures, the Briton called out—" What statues are those, driver?" "On the front of the Post Office ? " asked Pat, from between his coat collar. They are the twelve Apostles, your honour." "Twelve Apostles," muttered the Briton, con- temptuously; "there are only three there." Lord bless your sowl, sir," was the response, "sure you would not have them all out this Murthering wet day." I myself heard one of them give a sharp and rather courteous reply, when call- ing to a gentlemen if he wanted a car; the latter said "no," he was able to walk. The jarvey answered—" May your honour long be able, but seldom willing."

Fortune sometimes comes ter der one what leasts expecks it, but it is more apt ter come ter de man what works fer it De wust boy don't al'ers turn out ter be de bes' man. I has know'd good boy's ter drag along an' finally amount ter suthin'. De wust lick I cher got Was from a man what didn't want ter hit me. Now I'se mighty kereful 'bout crowdin' a man. When a pusson says at he wants ter fight, yer's safe; but when he tells yer dat he doan want ter fight, den stop right war yer is. DECEIT and falsehood, whatever convenience they may for a time promise or produce, are in the sum of life obstacles to happiness. Those who profit by the cheat distrust the deceiver; and the act by Which kindness was sought puts an end to confidence.

div.head: BOLTON ATROCITY. EXECUTION OF MACDONALD AT liIIIKDALE,
div.p: THE BOLTON ATROCITY. EXECUTION OF MACDONALD AT liIIIKDALE,

Thomas Macdonald, who waS Convicted at the last Liverpool Assizes of the atrocious murder of Elizabeth Amil Mit, a schoohnistress, was hanged in Kirkdale Gaol on Tuesdaf. hinrder for which he has paid )he extreme penalty of the law was committed on the 10th of November. On the morning of that day Miss Holt, who was a young and attractive woman, left her home to ful- fil her regular duties as assistant mistress at the National Schools, Belmont, near Bolton. She never reached the school-house, and on the following Saturday her mangled remains were found hidden under some bracken and leaves at the bottom of a ravine known as Longworth Clough. Suspicion at once fell upon Macdonald, a native of the village in which Miss Holt lived with her mother and sister. Macdonald—who bore the worst possible character—had been released only comparatively recently from penal servitude for an outrage upon a young woman, and had since then narrowly escaped being put upon his trial for the murder of a companion. The police felt sure from the first that they had the right man in custody; but Macdonald simplified matters at the coroner's inquiry by making a complete and circumstantial confession. It was thought at first that Miss Holt had been outraged as well as murdered; but happily the medical evidence contradicted this as- sumption, and Macdonald himself swore that such was- not the case. At the trial before Mr. Justice Cave, the prisoner, although he formally pleaded not guilty, exhibited great impatience at any prolongation of the proceedings, and when Mr. Cottingham, his counsel, pleaded for his life, Macdonald exclaimed," I don't want it. lam guilty straight off. . Let it drop." Mr. Cot- tingham submitted that the crime was a sudden impulse of passion ; there was no premeditation and no prepara- tion for it, for the prisoner had no weapon with him. He followed and caught hold of the girl, who struck him a severe blow across the face with her umbrella, and this exasperating him he closed with her, knocked her down, and then kicked her to death with his clogs. Mr. Justice Cave, of course, said there had been no excuse for the crime, and passed sentence of death in the usual form, after which Macdonald, still stolid and indifferent, turned lightly on his heel and jauntly stepped from the dock, whence he was conducted o the cells. After his condemnation he wrote to friends alluding to his posi- tion, without, however, referring to the circumstances which brought him to the gallows. He, indeed seemed to regard his fate with the greatest indifference, nor were any efforts made to obtain a reprieve. Representatives of the press were admitted to witness the execution which took place in a coach-house. At a few minutes before eight o'clock Macdonald was placed ,on the drop. Berry was the executioner, and his task was accomplished before the clock struck the hour. The murderer trembled violently whilst the last preparations were being made. The usual inquest was held and the usual verdict returned. Since, his condemnation the murderer has written several letters to his relatives. Theyare of the kind usually written by inmates of the condemned cell, especially whop the crime has been one , of a more than usually horriblOharacter.

'THE EXAMINEIi:
SATURDAY, JANUARY 3, 1891.

IT is an observation which is as Two Points trite as it is true that a good deal of View. depends upon the point of view. A mountain seen from the base appears to be a very much different object from the same moun. tam nas seen from the summit. The two knights, in the story, quarrelled as to the devices on the suspended shield until it was disclosed that one was speaking of the converse and the other of the obverse side of the armour. Each was right—from his own point of view. We print this week an important letter from Mr. H. 'WHITHAM on the MGKINLEv Tariff Act, which has caused such a stir not only in the United States but this country. Mr. WHITHAM had pronounced views upon the question of Protection when he was in Warring- ton, and he is still sound upon the subject. He has not changed his mind, as some people predicted, through contact with" Fair Trade" as it is known on the other side of the Atlantic. Incidentally he makes statements which are in confict with the eulogies we sometimes hear of the United States. Since Mr. WHITIAAM'S letter came to hand, we have received a reprint of the address which Mr. ANDREW CARNEGIE, the American millionaire, recently delivered to the citizens of Dundee. Be speaks in praise of the United States,and of the Re- publican form of Government, but, as might be ex- pected, the points of view of the Ironworker and of the Iron King are somewhat different. Mr. CAR- NEGIE says :—" Dembcracy is the Government of the poor. Out of 84 senators, there are not. six who could be called rich; and of the whole of our 325 representatives—and I know most of them—you could scarcely name a man who has an independent income." Mr. WHITHAM, on the other hand, says :—" The senate, which may be compared to the British House of Lords as a pri- vileged obstructive body, are all rich, very rich men, and take every measure for keeping them- selves a compact law-making clique." Can it be that the millionaire counts no man rich who does not come somewhere near his standard, while the wage-earner looks upon all as rich who spend freely and reach senatorial glory? Is it a difference again of the point of view? Touching another issue,- Mr. CARNEGIE says all the charges of defal- cations and corruption have been falsified; whilst Mr. WHITHAM roundly asserts that—" The American Senate is about the biggest swindling body in existence." He adds, and this is a point of some moment—" As rich men, they act in collusion with Wall Street; they work hand in hand with every Syndicate and Trust." As confirmatory of the view which our correspondent takes, it should be stated that it is notorious that every care was taken to ascertain the opinions ana wishes of the various Trusts when the McKinley Bill was under consideration; cvhile the masses were dealt with as if their interests were of no consequence. Mr. CARNEGIE hasn't a word to say against the Tariff; he treats it as a mere matter of Inabbub between the " ins " and the "outs." It is sufficient for him to know that, whether it continue for two years or twenty years, it will enable him to still further feather his nest. The McKinley Act is avowedly a measure of Protection; and if the theories of the Protec- tionists were sound it ought to operatein the direc- tion of benefitting the people as a whole. But does it? That is the question. As Mr. WHITHAM shows, it has already caused a rise in the price of clothing, and other goods imported from abroad— the advance in some cases being over 50 per cent. What have English "Fair Traders," if there are any still left, to say about such a result? Their contention was that putting a tax on imported goods would have no effect whatever upon the consumer, as the tax would fall upon the exporter. In their shdrt-sightedness, they were unable to perceive that, if the exporter continued to sell to the country taxing him, he was bound as a business man to add the tax to the price of the article exported, thus causing the tax to fall finally upon the consumer. Fortunately, the people of this country were too conscious of the blessings of Free Trade to be led away with a Will-o'the- Wisp ; and Protection, Reciprocity, Fair Trade, which were the various aliases of the commercial vagabond, have been driven from the platform, never again, it is to be hoped, to obtain a footing. Another thing which used to be insisted upon was that a protective tax would so stimulate home manufactures as to cause wages to rise ; but, so far from this being the result of the McKinley Tariff, Mr. WHITHAM names a number of places in which wages have already gone down. He does not say that this is in consequence of the new Act; but if wages are going down, whatever the cause, it cannot be said that the Act is caus- ing them to rise. But apart from any direct fall. the workman suffers, even if wages are the same, if there is a considerable rise in the prices of the articles which he uses. Mr. WHITHAM's estimate is that, in his own case, the effect of the Act is equivalent to a reduettion in his wages of at least one dollar a week. Who then does the Act benefit? it will be asked; and the answer is—the manufacturers whose particular goods are " roc' tected." Individuals will grow .richer, but the

div.p: people as a whole will be poorer. Take the ease of clothing: Let us assume that next year, as a consequence of the extra tax, American citizens have to pay one million-more for what they wear— for the goods imported from other countries. It is clear that they are poorer to the extent of that one million, always assuming that the tax is not levied for revenue purposes pure and simple. But in addition to this there will be the extra payment Upon clothing manufactured in America—prices rising as they are intended to do, to protect home traders. It may thus happen that the inhabitants Will be mulcted of •a, second million sterling,and all the time they are being fleeced they will be told that it is done in the interest of home labour and for the benefit of the working-man. It is a fortu- nate thing for the United States that she is pos- sessed of vast material resources, or she would have gone under as a result of these raids of the capitalists upon the earnings of the masses. But the plundering process may be attempted once too often; and the reicent elections show that the agricultural and other classes are having their eyes opened to the way in which they have been exploited. They are getting tired of paying more for everything in order that large manufacturers and the promoters of Tru.sts and Syndicates may become rich at express speed. They want to see something more of real fair trade; and with that object in view they are more then ever inclined to consider a Free Trade policy.
Mr. CONINGSBY DISRAELI pos- The Juvenile sessea a name which will be useful Plunger. to him; an.€l he is not lading
in audacity; but, unlike his late uncle, his
audacity is' in inverse ratio to his abi- lity. He has no ideas of his own, but le Is filled to the brim with the random assertions

which take the place of argument amongst the Tories who live in an atmosphere of "irresponsible frivolity." He has been addressing the electors oi High Legh ; and he treated them as creatures who dwelt in a. wild out-of-world place, ready to swal- low anything in the way of political statement Which anybody might offer them. Mr. Kenealy, of "Sir Roger" fame, once convulsed the House of Commons by speaking of himself as a lion about to shake the dew-drops from his mane; and the junior DISRAELI would seem to have had some- thing of the kind in his mind when he commenced .Lis speech, on Monday, by suggesting that ho Wag about to " attack the electors in their lair." Pro. evading to chant the praises of the Government, he immediately" gave himself away," by stating that the establishment of ,a Board of Agriculture Was "by far the most important Act ever passed for agriculture." The farmers who heard this must have rubbed their eyes, and wondered if they had been asleep whilst the good things of the new Board had been showered upon them. They may look and look again, and they will find that the most important work which the Board has yet accomplished has been the muzzling of all dogs in this district—except sporting dogs. Still, accord- ing to Mr. DisnAnti,the Board has a great mission: for" it must and would cope with the distressing fall of prices for 'produce which farmers had ex- Perienced of late years." There now I Who will then deny that the Tories are the farmer's friends --after that? The prices of produce are to be raised ; for it is not to be supposed that when the irory candidate for Altrincham talks of coping with their "distressing fall" that he means them to be brought lower. That would be to " relieve " the distressed by insult and injury. So the Board " must and would ' raise prices. Oats and wheat, hay and straw, and butter and eggs are to be coped with by the Board of agriculture until Prices shall rise and the farmer's eyes shall dance With joy. Mr. DISRAELI has spoken, and will .he not keep his word? He has visited the wilds of Cheshire, and "attacked the electors in their lair," and this is what has come of it. " Wonder- ' 1111 and, yet again wonderful ;" but it would be just a little more satisfactory if the new evangelist Would condescend to explain how it is to be done. It will be awkward if the farmer, after parting with his vote, should discover that nothing is " done" except the farmer himself. Let the voters asked the Juvenile Plunger if he has any authority for making such an unheard-of promise. Perhaps it will turn out to be no more reliable than the statement that " the Conservative party had never thought fit to put trust in Mr. PARNELL ? " "What ziever ? " Has he no recollection of the election of 1885 when the Conservatives put every trust in )4-r• PARNELL, and secured the pA.RNELLITE vote Item one end of the kingdom to the other? Has ho fever heard of the interview which the late Lord CARNARVON, as a member •of Lord SAMS- Ittrivirg Government, had with Mr. PARNELL and that too with Lord SALISBURY'S sanction? But Perhaps all this took place before the Juvenile was L ,"°lll—pGlitically speaking. The Plunger would :utve us believe too that "the whole Irish question uas been one of fraud and disgusting idiocy and the present Prime Minister, to say nothing of any Other, stands there Tore utterly Condemned. Lord `l•Liainairt- was certainly party-to a promise made t° the Irish people, through Lord RANDOLPH eUDRCHILL, that the Irish question should be aettled by "similarity and simultaneity " in .„14°Cal Self-Government Bills for England and Ire- :and. That promise has not been kept; and perhaps 11 is not too strong to speak of it as a." fraud." o say nothing however about "disgusting 41i0cy"; it is not the sort of language we should think of applying to Lord SALISBURY, strongly as 70 disapprove of his way of dealing with "the whole question:" Perhaps it does not apply to any- or anybody; and must simply be taken to be the Juvenile Plunger's way of" swearing at large," after promising at large.

F There is a weak point about Emin Pasha; he doesn't get along with the Germans any more than he did with Stanley, and he has been recalled. He has had too much of his own way in "bossing " it for years on the Upper Nile. He doesn't take kindly to orders, after giving orders so long, and goes beetle-catching when he should be acting on instructions.

Runcorn is moving on the question of technical instruction. The Act has been adopted; the matter was referred to by Mr. Brunner M.P., at a meeting on Monday, and was under the considera- tion of the Board of Commissioners on Tuesday. It will be the tam next of the Town Council of Warrington; and it is to bo hoped the members Will show themselves equal to the occasion.

The' weatUr van OR the Warrington Town ,Clock toppled over on Monday night. It is i'unioured that it came down because it couldn'i stand the severe weather—especially the bitter blast of Monday night. Another suggestion is that it has been over-elevated" during the fes- tire season; and, like sundry citizens whom it has looked down upon, it has had recourse to an it orly English attitude,"

The Emperor of. Germatly Ain ghtigs his amn gate" He has parted with his Oltivricellor—tAe Chalicellor---and now he has dropped Or. Stoeker, the Court Chaplain. His head is full tif new ideas, and lila pace is so quick that the old stager annot keep op with him. Ile will meet, of coutse, • with difficaies and obstructions, but it is to be hoped he will not "come a cropper," and turn back as so many Royal Reformers have done.

The liberal Unionists suffer a loss by the death of Mr. T. Richards, member for Hartlepool, while Sir Savile Crossley, member for Lowestoft Divi- sion, has j ust announced his intention of rat iring at the neA tlection.
Thej,are going off, the friends we knew, There going one by one; And if the General Election is delayed until 1892 —well, there will be very few left to go.

The Thatpes is frozen over at Windsor, but it has been kept open by the traffic in the neighbour- hood of London. The last great fair on the royal river was in the winter of 1813 and 'l4; and the first frost fak of which there is any record was in 695. It was expected that the frost of 1879-80 would result in a fair, but it " just missed." The frost that year lasted from November 22nd, 1879, to February 211 d, 1880. The winter of 1881 was, it may be added, also very severe.

There are signs at the Government offices that the elections may take place next year. Estimates are being prepwed already with a view to an unusually early ludget. The Ministry will in all probability " ridefor a fall," seeing that the split in Ireland softens the ground for them. But a good many things may happen before March— amongst others tht reconsolidation of Liberals in Ireland and in gland;Eo and in that case the Government will dePida to flounder on as long as • they can.

" 'Tis not in mortis to command success ;" but the railway servants ill Scotland certainly deserve it. Whilst the eight-ours day is being discussed they have actually to strike to obtain a day of ten hours. Shame on thi Railway Companies who resist this reasonable pioposal, and shame on out- siders who fail to give the men their sympathy and aid. Railway-men ought to be in one great Union, and, with a genoral strike, success would be certain. They shoull take a lesson from the miners.

Therg was a pathetic lido scene at the Newton Polioe Courton Saturday. A boy named Woods, of bad character, was foutd guilty of theft, and sentenced to ten days' imprilonment,to be followed by five years' detention in a reformatory. Mother and child clung to each othT and cried over each other, the mother declaring la.t "all her children had been sent to reformatorid• They must have been a bad lot; but it is iniPossible not to feel sorry for the mother thus deprived of the company of her offspring.

There is one advantage in IPing "run in" at various places; you get to knowthe most comfort- able gaols. A hawker named 118, who was re- manded, at Warrington, on Tudday, on a charge of burglary,demanded that he shoald be remanded to Walton, where he would be better treated than at Warrington.; but he didn't get ins way. It is a pity that a person of such exact Icnowledge and nice sensibility shoulA have any reason to complain. Why not lodge him at the Lion,whilst on remand, and let him have a festive time of it ? The Watch Commiteee must see to making the bridewell more inviting.

A London Correspondent says may in- terest Mr. Cavendish-Bentinck to know that the city church of St. George's, which he desires to save from destruction, had a congregation op Christmas Day not so large as the surpliced choir. At St. Michael's, Wood-st., another doomed church, the entire congregation was six persons, of witi three were children." This item of news may be com- mended to the attention of the Rev. G. S. Reaney, who has recently expressed his views on the atten- dance at Congregational Church meetings.. per- haps he will explain whether tho congregs!ign of six persons means that the church was too high" or too "low." Or could it be suffering froni "the dissidence of Dissent ?"

Shakespeare says there is "a soul of good in things evil." There is a soul of good in Mr. 'Alter Scott, secretary of the Mather-lane Cotton Spinning Co. ( Leigh), notwithstanding his defalcations and hurried departure to Cape Colony. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

We give this week a humourous pictorial repre- sentation of the principal events of the year which ended on Wednesday last; and we purpose sup- plying, weeic by week, portrait sketches of the most notable men who have died during the past year, accompanying the portraits with brief bio- graphies. We shall commence next week with the late King of Holland and the late Sir Edgar Boehm.
There is a strike At Birmingham in the coffin trade; but what of that? What most people want to see is a successful strike in the coughing business.

Professor Cohn has published some statistics which show that German school children are be- coming shortsighted. It is the result of the operation of the law of compensation ; they gain learning and lose eyesight. As they become long- headed, they grow shortsighted, and nature pre- serves her balance.

A contemporary says that at Wick, in the North of Scotland roses and all sorts of flowers "are in bloom in the gardens, and full-grown strawberries may be plucked in the open air. "All sorts of flowers is decidedly vague, and suggests all sorts of story-telling. It is to be feared that there• is somebody at Wick with a wicked imagination.

div.head: FATAL BRAWL AT NORTHWICH.
div.p: THE FATAL BRAWL AT NORTHWICH.

At Northwich, on Thursday morning, Elizabeth Caries, 16, and Ellen Lyden, 17, were charged befote Mr. Brunner, 11. P., with causing thekleath of Sabina Naughton, an old woman. It was alleged that dur- ing a drunken brawl on Christmas Day the pri- soners knelt on the deceased, who died on Sunday from peritonitis, which the doctor said might have resulted from violence. Prisoners, against whom the coroner's jury returned a verdict of manslaugh- ter, were remanded. CRITMILEY, High Class Tailor, Bold-st. Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: DEATH OP MRS. SHONE OF RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH OP MRS. SHONE OF RUNCORN.

Many of our readers will learn with -ie-g-r-et--nf o'4 61:',..ath of Mrs. Shone, wife of Mr. George Shone, Of tile Devon- shire Hotel. Mrs. Shone succumbed to disease from which she has suffered for several Mcs, having only attained the age of 39 -years. Ins htl. early life Mrs. Shone was a teacher at the National, De.y Schools, and she was highly rospeeted by a wide, tircle of friends. She was interred at the Cemetery yesterday amid many demon- stra.tions of regret . PIRQBABLE APPOINTMENT FOR A LOCAL MANUFACTURER.

The" Railway Herald "says :—There are to be great changes in the personnel of the London and North-Western Company with the New -Year. Sir Richard Moon will retire, as no doubt, all our readers are aware, and will, be succeeded in the chairmanship by Lord Stalbridge. In addition to this, other retirements from the Board are mooted, and it is said that Mr. Dennis, of the firm of J. H. Dennis and Co., of Liverpool and Widnes, is likely to be selected to fill one of the vacant seats. NEW YEAR'S DAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. Thursday the first day of the year 1891, was observed as a holiday by the tradesmen of these towns, and the various offices were clossd at noon. Work was continued as usual at the chemical manufactories. The railway companies issued tickets for Liverpool at a cheap rate, and there was a great exodus of the people to that city to witness the pantomine and the opera. Although a thaw had set in skaters thronged the pits in the neigh- bourhood, and appeared to greatly enjoy themselves.

UNITED ALKALI COMPANY, LIMITED. We have already announced (says the "Liverpool Journal of Commerce ") that this company have taken offices in Exchange-buildings. We now understand that Mr. Edward Mount, secretary to the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, Limited, has been appointed assistant secretary to this Union; and Mr. Edward, salesman to Messrs. Pilkington and Sons, Widnes, and Mr. Banister, who occupied a similar position with Muspratt Brothers and Huntley, Limited, have been appointed salesmen to the new company.

div.head: FROST AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE FROST AT RUNCORN.

After a fortnight's severe frost, a rapid thaw set in early on New Year's Day, and was hailed with much satisfaction in the neighbourhood of Runcorn and Widnes where the canal traffic has been serioully inter- fered with, and much loss has been caused. On Wed- nesday afternoon the steam tug "Runcorn," while attempting to break the ice on the Weston Canal, damaged her bow and sank, and the engineer had a narrow escape from drowning. Should the mild weather continue traffic will resume its ordinary course to-day.

div.head: BAPTIST SALE OF • WORK AT WIDNES.
div.p: BAPTIST SALE OF • WORK AT WIDNES.

The annual Sale of Work and Christmas ;free in con- nection with the Widnestaptist Chapel, was held on New Year's Day. There were three tastefully set-out stalls and the ladies commenced their disposal at three o'clock without any formality. Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss M.P., had consented to perform the opening ceremony, though through being in London he was unable to carry out his intention, but did not forget to forward a donation. In the evening entertainments were organised, and were well patronised. The Chapel debt was seduced £2O by the effort.

There died at Widnes Accident Hospital, yesterday, a married woman named Ellen Moat, who had resided at 3, Farrant-street. °tithe evening of the '26th ult., she had been to a friend'shouse in Grenfell-etreet, in order to fetch home her husband who was under the influence of drink. When returning home she fell down on the slippery pavement and sustained a compound fracture of the leg. The bone was set by Dr. McCambridge., and the woman was thearemoved in the horse ambulance to the hospital, whetre she remained until her death under the care of Dr. McDonnell. THE ANNUAL DANCE AT GIESWOOD HALL. FINANCE. -PROPOSED INCREASE OF SALARY.

The Finance Committee reported receipts amounting to £lB2 14s. lid., and recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £302 19s. 4d. The Committee recommended that the salary of the Law Clerk be in- creased from £llO to £135 a year, to date from January Ist 1891.—Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the minutes and explained that the Board bad made application to the Local Government Board for sanction to the payment of £5O to the Law Clerk for extra services. A reply had been received stating that they could not sanction the payment. The money had been earned, and the Com- mittee considered that the only way by which they could discharge their just obligation was by an increase of salary.—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion.—Mr. Meadowcroft pointed out that according to the Com- missioners Clauses Act, before such a resolutio.a could bpassed, the resolution fixing the maximum salary of the Law Clerk- at £llO must be rescinded. After some discussion the minute was withdrawn and Mr. Imison gave notice that he would move the required resolution at the next meeting. THE LIBRARY.

On the minutes of the Library Committee coming up for confirmation, Mr. Humphreys said it would be a dis- tinct advantage to the Library Committee if the Chair- man or Vice-chairman of the Committe3 were a member of the Board. At the present time it was left to any in- dividual member to take charge of any resolution of the Committee.—The Chairman pointed out this was a mat- ter for the Library Committee to deal with. _ TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION ACT. _
Mr. Meadowcroft had given notice that he would move :—" That this Board do not put into operation the powers of the Technical Education Act until the School

Board are able to provide int;r-niedLLOr-s;COrTci;r-ied—u-- cation for the middle classes of the town." He said he was placed in a queer position through the proceedings which took place on the 18th inst., and which he con- sidered entirely irregular, and contrary to the provisions of the Act under which that Board conducted its busi- ness. He could not refuse to recognise that the Board had come to a decision notwithstanding the objections he raised, and he felt that if he moved his resolution he might place the Board in an awkward position through the course already adopted,from which he entirely dissented. He had no wish to compromise the Board, nor desire to injure any steps which in the opinion of the Committee ought to be conducive to the interests of the town. If

the Board discharged their duties efficiently, the respon- sibilities of the Act were serious, and as the Board had adopted the Act in principle, it was to be hoped the Board would not skirk their responsibilities as other Boards had done, but would be prepared to administer the Act themselves, and to assist secondary or interme- diate education, which had a strong claim upon the rate- payers of the country at the present day. He withdrew his trtotien,----Mr, Liglitburn explained that the special , inivAliiN was held oti 913 18th, iicause notiee wag to be , given to the County Council by the 20th.—Mr. Hum- phreys said at the present time the School Board had not power to provide secondary education, but under the elastic terms of the Technical Instruction Act the teaching could include such subjects as short- hand, typewriting, commercial history, geography, French, German, Italian, Portugese, commercial calculation, coth:nercial correspondence, mechanical engineeringonathematics. and Mr. Humphreys argued that this was practically secondary education.—Mr. Imison said Mr. Mmdowcroft gave notice of his motion under a misapprehension, because it was definitely said that under the Technical Education Instruction Act they could not establish a commercial ' school for the middle classes. He observed that the member for the division (Mr. Brunner), the other night mentiunede that the establishment of such a school was a very proper object for their support, and that he hoped something would at last be done for the interest of the middle classes. After further discussion the subject dropped.

div.head: KINDNESS TO INMATES.
div.p: KINDNESS TO INMATES.

The Master reported that Mrs. Soulby,of Runcorn, had given the children of the House a tea and Christmas tree on the 17th December on which occasion the Rv.J. Hol- den brought his musical troupe. Christmas gifts had been received from Sir Richard Brooke, Mr. H. Talbot, Mr. Mclntyre, Mr. Heywood, Mrs. Marsden, Miss Best, Mr. Kidd, Mrs. Wright and the Chaplain had lent Chinese lanterns. Periodicals had been supplied during the past year by Lady Greenall, Mr. Aaron, and Superin- tendent Large. The Guardians had provided tobacco for which he wanted 10s. 6d. (Mr. Bra,ndreth at once collected 14s. 6d. from the members present.) Mr. Speakman moved a vote of thanks to the donors. He thought it ought to be specially mentioned that Mrs. Soulby and her pupils had given an entertainment by which she raised about £l3, which had been spent in giving the inmates a treat, which afforded them un- bounded pleasure. The life of the children in the house. was happy in its way but anything that threw a gleam of sunshine across their path as Mrs. Soulby's kindness had done would never be forgotten by them.—,The motion was seconded by Mr. Tanner and carried unanimously.

div.head: WATER FOR FRODSRAM.
div.p: WATER FOR FRODSRAM.

The Fredsham Parochial Committee reported that con- sideration of the water supply for Frodshain had been deferred for a month.—Mr. Thomas said the Gas Coin. pa.ny had made up their minds not to carry out their Act and supply Frodsham with water, and as water was so much wanted, it would be a pity te waste time. ; There was plenty of water s.t Overton, bat it was in Main-st. and in the township that water was really re- quire& He moved that a Committee, consisting of Messrs. RESIGNATION OF THE CLERK. The itssistant Clerk said the resolution of the authority with regard to the resignation of the .clerk had been -submitted to his father, who however wished the assia- ant clerk to be appointed as a special favour to himself as he did not feel that he could take the .position any longer.—The Chairman said Mr. Linaker's services had been very useful .to the authority, and they all regretted very much that he could not continue clerk. However there was nothing for it but to appoint the assistant -clerk according to law.—Mr. Thomas asked if they could not appoint a deputy.—The Assistant Clerk said there was mopower to appoint a deputy.—Mr. Whitlow asked if they *were legally bound to appoint the assistant at the -same salary as before.—The Assistant Cleric : At such salary as is decided upon.—The Chair- man -said there was no fiwed salary: it was decided at the end,dfeach year.—Mr _ Brandreth : IMS a year. 'He asked supposing Mr. Linaker in some little time resigned the Clerkship to the Guardians would that dissolve this appciintment to the Rural Sanitary Authority.— The Chairman-: I think it would.—The Assistant-Clerk: You would have to ask the Local Government Board. fie added that as long as he remained Assistant-Clerk tothe Guardian& he could retain the Clerkship to the Authority. ' —Mr. Knowles said it was hard that they skould be told they must appoint a man whether they would or not.— Mr. Heywood,: I don't think we have anything to do with the appointment of a rnan.—The Assistant-Clerk,: tt is the act .you have simply to go upon.—The Chair- man-: And the Act says the assistant-clerk shall be ap- pointed.—Mr.trandreth : We will not make an appoint- ment.—The Aseistant-Clerk : You are still without clerk. You are hound to pass a resolution.—Mr. Whitlow : It is just the same as many other things under the Local Government Board. We must find the money-and they must tell us how to spend it.—Mr. Thomas moved that the AsAstant-Clenk (Mr. H. G. Linaker) be appointed Clerk to the Authority, and it Was carried.

ported that they were too near the school and house, and that the accommodation was insufficient. —The matter was referred to the Medical Officer.

CABAL BOATS ACTS. Tbelnspector presented his annual report under Canal Boats Acts. He said the total number of canal boats inspected while passing through the district of the Rural Sanitary Authority was 86. The amount of remunera- tion paid to the Inspector was £lO per annum. ,The general condition of the boats and their oecupants was very much improved since the passing of the Acts. There were very few children of school age on board the single boats: but they were still to be found on board those worked in pairs. No legal proceedings had been taken during the past year.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

The other day, Joseph Stanneri aged 50 years, an enploy6 of the Manchespr Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater undertaking), had covered some wagons at, the docks with sheets and jumped off in front of a train, which he did not perceive. The wagons.passed over him and severed both legs from his body. He was conveyed with all speed to the railway station, and dispatched to Liverpool, but he died before his arrival there. THE LOCKOUT AT GARSTON.

• There is little change ti) report in the position of matters at Garston. The railway Company show no disposition to yield, but it is rumoured among the men that they intend to give the loading and ! discharging of vessels into the hands of stevedores, and in that way there will be a chance for the strikers to get back again. The railway company have several hundred imported men carrying on the necessary work in connection with the loading and discharging of vessels in the docks. The great bulk of these are now in the permanent employment of the company, and reside with their families in Liverpool. They proceed to and frotn their work in trains running to Garston Docks. The company pay in wages to those men from -1750 to £l,OOO a week. All this money was formerly spent among the tradespeople of Garston, but, as nearly all of it is now sperit elsewhere, the loss to the local shop- keepers is very great. Although the distress at Garston has been in a measure mitigated by Christ- mas liberalities, there are still many families in want. A population of some 2,000 is still affected by the recent loss of work, in spite of the fact that many of the more, skilled men have obtained employ- ment elsewhere..
