div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COIMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COIMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were present Messrs. Fisher,White, Imison, Pritchard, Grice,Abel, Lightburn, Meadowcroft, Wiswall, II umphreys, Haukinson, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshal/ (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). HIGHWAYS ANV3ITILDINGS COMMITTEE.

This Committee reciimmended that the tender of Messrs. Wilson and Sefton for the cutting and laying of a pipe sewer in Heath-road at the following prices be accepted :—Frona B to Don plan, 163. per lineal yard; from D to E, lls, per lineal yard ; from Eto A, 78. ner lineal yard; and for the brickwork of manhole, 4s. 6d. per sup.yard of nine inch work. That anarch in continua- tion of the Viaduct at Victoria-road in course of erection by the Manchester Ship Canal Co. be constencted in ac- cordance with plan submitted ; also a length of sewer at the above-named road ; and that public notice be given inviting tenders for the execution of the works. That the scavengers be provided with overcoats, and that the tender of Mr. D. Jones to supply eleven overcoats for the sum of £8 10s. be accepted. That the following scavengers have their wages increased from 16s. to 18s. -per week, viz :—J. Williams, T. Hart, W. Worrall, and S. Chrimes. That the plan of Messrs. W. Farrell and Son for the erection of a Joiner's shop, saw mill, and stable at the lower end of Hope-st. be approved.—Mr. Fisher. moved the adoption of the minutes, and explained that there were six arches in the Viaduct connecting Victoria- road with Will Brow. The Ship Canal Company were putting up five arches on, their OWE land, but the sixth would be on land belonging to Major Orred, and it was only reasonable that the company should wish the Board to construct that arch.—Mr. Pritchard said during the recent snowstorms the leading footpaths in the town had beenin a most deplorable condition. He thought they ought to be cleared immediately after every snow- storm, and not allowed to become frozen and hard and have to be cleared by picks. Mr. Humphreys asked whether it would net be pcssible by means of byelaws to adopt a plan whereby the property owners or occupiers should be under an obligation to clear away the snow opposite their respective premises. —The Chairman said they already had a byelaw but it had never been enforced.—Mr. Barter: The Act provides for it being done.—Mr. Fisher said the falls of snow were so frequent that they would have required a tre- mendous big staff to clear every footpath, and have found at the end of the year that they were short of cash. As to Mr. Humphreys' suggestion,lit was putting a duty i upon householders that would be scarcely just to them, , and he would not support it.. They paid rates and it , mould not be reasonable to make them scavengers.—Mr. Grice agreed, and said it was the duty of the Authority to keep the streets in proper order.—Mr. Meadowcroft • commented upon the filthy condition of the streets, and ,said he had repeatedly looked for the scavengers but had not been able to find them. He had no notion where , they located themselves.—The Surveyor: They are al- ways somewhere.—Mr. Meadowcroft agreed with Mr. Humphreys, and said he failed to see any hardship in each householder clearing the snow away from his own premises.—Mr. Lightburn : How about my house ?-1111r. Meadowcroft: I should not take yours to be in a public thoroughfare.—The Chairman: Sf you force it upon one occupier don't let one go free.—Mr. Meadowcroft referring to ,the scavengers said they ought to get a better class of men for that wage without giving an overcoat.—Mr. Fisher said it had been usual to supp ly overcoats, the total cost of which was £8 103. There were ten scavengers but only four were increased,because these tour were the men Mr. Barkerha,d to depend upon for extraordinary work.—Mr. Wis wall said Mr. Meadow- croft asked that attention should be paid to expenditure. He was sorry that Mr. Meadowcrott did not attend the committee meeting. No one on the Board knew better than he did the duties of the surveyor,and Mr.,Barker had to depend upon these men for many things besides scavenging, in which great care had to bo exercised. He was as carefgel as any member need be as regarded expenses and the economic working of the town, and he was sorry Mr. Meadowcroft did not attend the committee meeting where these subjects were discussed.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: TKr *CANAL BOATS ACTS.
div.p: TKr *CANAL BOATS ACTS.

The minutes of ther.Canal Boats Committee contained the annual report as to the execution of the Canal Boats Acts. It stated that during the year Ff*g• h t boats had been registered, making a total of 90:i registered in Run- corn. 'There had been SI contraventions of the Acts reported by the inspector., and the Oommitte.e had care- fully examined each ease. The Authority had satisfied itself that the cOntraventions had been effectually remedied by means of the Notice Forms, which are found to be an efficacious modeof dealing with infringements. There had been no case of infectious disease reported by the Inspector, nor any been notified from any boat under the Infectious Disease (Notification) Act, 1889, Durinc,, the year the Inspector had found 429 men, 125 women, and 126 children on board the boats inspected. He was desired by the Local Authority to say that they were of opinion, judging from their Inspector's written and ver- bal reports, that there was a continued improvement in the condition of the persons engaged in canal boat traffic. It had been noticeable . during the year that female labour had decreased, and that the labour of young men had been substituted. There was also a dis- tinct improvement in the sanitary condition of the boats. There had been 306 inspections made during the year. The salary of the Inspector was £2O per annum. with an allowance of 2s. per boat examined for registration. The rz port was adopted.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY "AN OCCASIONAL COURESPONDENT."

A reference to the file of the" Examiner" has revealed that the treat to the aged people of Run- corn never included the word" poor" in its title. As the report of the first treat states, " age was the only passport," and the limit then as now was fixed at 60 years. A meeting of the Committee took place on Monday evening, and arrangements were made for carrying out the treat on a scale of equal magnitude with any past occasion, and there is no doubt that subscriptions will be forthcoming from a generous public to enable the Committee to realise their aim. Fortunately the severe weather has broken up, and there appears to be no need at present for the soup kitchen which has been men- tioned.

By the death of Mr. John Dickson, at the age of 60 years, a familiar figure has been removed from Widnes. A native of Cumberland, Mr. Dickson spent his early life in Warrington, and 33 years ago, when quite a young man,- established himself in business in Widnes as a chemist and druggist. He took a deep interest in local affairs, became a mem- ber of the Local Board, and was placed in the honourable position of chairman. Eighteen years ago, he retired from business and resigned his -seat on the Board, and became the Sanitary Inspector of the town, his professional knowledge making him a most efficient official. In religion he was a Church- man, and for many years was churchwarden of the Parish Church.and on his retirement the parishioners acknowledged his services appropriately, In pri- vat.e life 11.3 was much esteemed.; and his sudden demise will be widely regretted. In the space of three weeks, in fact on Monday, the 26th of the present month, Runcoinians will have the privilege of listening to the great London preacher, the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, M.A. His visit will be in connection with the London Mis- sion, which has done a marvellous amount of work of a social and religious character, and of which the rev, gentleman is the guiding spirit. It is intended that Mr. Hughes will preach in the afternoon, and in the evening address a monstre public meeting.

div.head: WOUNDING OASES AT WIDNES.
div.p: WOUNDING OASES AT WIDNES.

Mr. H. Wade Deacon was engaged at Widnes Police Court, for four hours yesterday investigating several charges of unlawful wounding. Edward !Tynan, labourer of Nelson-st., was committed to the Quarter Sessions for stabbing a companion named Michael J. Keeghan, of Wellington-st. On Christmas Eve the two men were drinking together in various public-houses and at closing time went to the house of the prisoner's father. Here they commenced a wordy quarrel which developed into blows. The prisoner threatened to kill Keeghan and going into his own house, he returned with aknife with which he twice stabbed him, inflicting a serious wound on the arm and the shoulder. Keeghan fell down from loss of blood and was conveyed to Dr. Hutchinson's : surgery where his wounds were dressed. In a second case James Mosal, of Water-st., was charged with intending to do grievous bodily harm to John Twick. • The men are Poles and reside in Water-st. On Saturday night they met in the house of a friend named William Steed, and the prosecu- tor returned the prisoner 10s. which he had received on the understanding that he obtained employment for him but had failed to do so. Afterwards they commenced a dispute, which ended in blows, and the prisoner being handed a poker, struck the pro- secutor a blow on the forehead which stunned hini. He was taken from the house to Dr. Hutchinson's sergery. An interpreter had to be employed in this case and the prisoner was committed for trial. • Rose Ann Mooney, of Nelson-st., was remanded until Monday on a charge of wounding Michael Costello.—Superintendent Noblett stated that the prosecutor and his wife occupied apartments and they were seated in their rooms on Saturday night. Cohen the prisoner entered, and picking up a brass candlestick, struck the prosecutor on the head and face with it several times. He lost a great quantity of blood and Dr. Hutchinson ordered his removal to the Hospital.

div.head: PRESCOT BOA RD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOA RD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon when there were present, Major J. NV. Wareing (Chairman),Rey. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. W. Tyrer' C. B. Lowe, NV. Middlehurst, J. Goldsworth, Burrows,Peover, Ranson, J. Mercer, Jas. Burchall, Ken- wright, Graves, P. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) THE COMPLIMENTS OF THE SEASON.---The Chairman, said before they Commenced business business he wished the members of the Board the compliments of the season. He hoped the year they were just entering upon would be a happy and prosperous one for all. (Applause.) Mr. Middlehurst said he was sure the Board reciprocated the feeling expressed by the Chairman. RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 614 inmates this week, 619 last week and 575 in the cor- responding week last year. There had been 61 vagrants against 51 last year. He also reported the receipt of pre- for the use of the inmates from Mr. Wm. Blinkhorn (Sutton), Mrs. Webster (St. Relens), Mr. R. G. Brook, messrs. W. Halsall and Son (Prescoty, Mr. J. R. Borrows (St. Helens), and Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens). On the motion of Mr. Middlehurst, seconded by Mr. Davies, a vote of thanks was tendered to the givers. Borrnn AND MARGARINE.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the action of the t Guardians in obtaining for the consumption of the Work- house inmates in lieu of the butter hitherto allowed, half the quantity of butter and an equal quantity of mar- garine of good quality. VACCINATION AT RAINFORD.—The Local Government , Board wrote stating that they had received a report from their inspector, Mr. Thompson, after his recent inspection of public vaccination in the Prescot Union, in which he stated that Mr. Andrew Murdock, public vac- cinator for Rainford district, vaccinated children in two places only, insteadef making such insertions as would peoduce at least four good sized vesicles, as required by ' Article 2of the official instructions. The results were 133, no means satisfactory. The Guardians were requested to obtain and forward to the Board an explanation of the public vaccinator's conduct.—The Clerk stated that he had sent a copy of the letter to Dr. Murdock, and he read a long reply from that gentleman, to the effect that he had adopted the course alluded to in consequence of the strong prejudice existing against four vaccination marks on the.mrt of the parents in his district. The Prejudice was now dying out, and la should in future insist cpl all children beingvaccinated in accordance with the regulations. TEE PROPOSED ASSISTANT RELIEVING OFFICER FOR WIDNES.—This matter was again brought forward on the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board , stating that the proper course was for the Guardians to appoint any competent person to assist Mr. Theacey in his duties, if they were more than he could efficiently discharge.—The Clerk said the difficulty was that the Guardians only wished to appoint him temporarily, pend- ing a rearrangement of the relief districts.—The letter was ultimately referred to the Special Committee having charge of the subject. This was the principal business.

div.head: AN ENGINE DRIVER'S FATALITY.
div.p: AN ENGINE DRIVER'S FATALITY.

On Monday forenoon, before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner of South-west Lancashire, an in- quest was held at the St. Helens Town Hall, on the body of John larsden, 31 years of age, of 153, Al- bion-5r., who died on Christmas Day from injuries received on the 30th january last,whilst following his em- ployment as an engineer at the w -irks of Messrs.Canning- ton, Shaw, and Co.. glass-bottle makers. Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, represented the firm. Mrs. Marsden, widow, gave evidence of identification, and while doing so, she swooned, and had to be carried from the Court, Frederick Atkinson, manager, said he saw the deceased standing on the framework of an engine unscrewing a , nut for the purpose of easing some bearings which had got hot. He thought the screw-key must have slipped, as he fell into the flywheel. He was severely injured, and was taken to the hospital. In conversation with the deceased, the latter had said it was his own fault. Geo. Armytage, foreman mechanic, said deceased should not have repaired the machinery or engine without first re- porting the matter to him (witness). The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Passenger train on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway which left Kirkdale for Liverpool shortly after seven o'clock on Thursday morning ran into a siding at Sandhills and came into -Collision with a number of coal waggons. 'The trucks were smashed aid several passen- gers were injured.
PENKETH.
CHRISTMAS PRESENTS.

During Christmas week Mr. G. H. Bolton, of Pen- keth House, generously presented a number of hot- pots, plum puddings, whisky, and a quantity of coal. These were distributed by several of Mr. Bolton's employs to all the widows of Penketh. DEATH OF AN OLD INHABITANT. Penketh's oldest inhabitant passed away yester- day week, in the person of Mrs. Whitfield, who had teached the advanced age of 92. The deceased lady came to Penketh some five or six years ago, and since that time has been well known to the residents. in the township. Considering her age, Mrs. Whit- field was a wonderfully active woman, and until about a fortnight ago was able to get about much as usual. Since that time, however, her strength has been gradually failing. The funeral took place on Sunday at Farnworth Church. WATCH NIGHT SERVICE. On Wednesday evening the annual tea party and entestainment in connection with the watch night service was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. Tea, which was prepared under the superintendence of Mrs. R. Garnett, was on the tables at 7.30 p.m. There was only a moderate attendance, numbering about 70. After tea an interesting programme con- sisting of addresses, readings, quartets, and con- tributions from the fife band, was gone through and greatly enjoyed. The watch night service was commenced at 11 o'clock and conducted by Mr. C. E. Parker.

div.head: WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.
div.p: WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.

In connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School, the annual tea party was given on Tuesday after- noon to the members of Miss Hughes's, Miss Rout- ledge's, and Miss Hobson's classes. Tea was pro- vided and prepared by the above-named teachers, and commenced at 4.30 P.m. Seventy scholars were present, and did full justice to the fare provided. At 5.30 tea was finished, and the room was cleared. Songs and recitations were given by several of the children, and afte•wards various "games were indulged in till 7.45. They were dismissed at eight o.clock, each of them receiving before leaving an orange, some gingerbreads, biscuits, sweets, and nuts. The proceedings were carried through in a satisfactory manner, the children dispersing -highly pleased with the afternoon's entertain- ment.

TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE. i On Monday evening, the annual treat to the aged people of Sankey and Penketh was held in the Con- servative Club-room, Stocks-lane. Invitations were issued to 97 of the old men and women, and 85 were able to avail themselves of the invitation. Twelve were unable to be present through sickness. Tea was served at 6.30 p.m., and all present did full justice to the good fare provided. The following ladies prepared the tea and presided at the tables:— Mesdames Routledge, R. Boardman, and Foster, and Misses Ruutledge, Thorpe, and Foster. An enter- tainment, provided by a number of friends, was subsequently given, the chair being occupied by Mr. J. C. Routledge. The programme consisted of songs, recitattons,violin solos,&c., Herr Praeger act- ing as accompanist. A recitation by Miss Flossy Watson, and a most amusing piece given in nigger costume by the Foster Bros. were greatly appreciated by the audience. llerr Praeger favoured the company with several violin solos. A song was contributed by Sergeant Donoghue, the Balaclava veteran. The following gentlemen constitute the Committee who had the management of the treat this year: Messrs. ' Routledge, Foster, Wilson, Longshaw, R. Boardman, J. Jackson, P. Boardman, Denton, and Thorpe; honorary secretary, Mr. J. Foster. Each of the old folk was presented on leaving with a small gift, the men receiving an ounce of tobacco and a pipe, and the women a quarter of tea. Those who were unable to be present had their tea and tobacco sent to them. At the conclusion of the programme, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Herr Praeger for his services at the piano, and a pleasant evening was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.

THE MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. Last evening week the annual conversazione in connection with the Mutual Improvement Associa- tion was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. There was a large attendance' of members and friends, numbering upwards of 130. Amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs. R. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. D. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. T. Gandy, Mr. and Mrs. Peers, Mr. J. Dignuni, Mr. J. T. Gumersall, Mr. W. J. Wig- field, Mr. R. E. Garnett, Mr. A. J. White, Mr. J. Atherton, and Mr. F. Hughes. The room was most tastefully • decorated for the occasion with ever- greenss• mottoes, pictures, &c., and reflected the highest credit on Messrs. Parker, White, Dunabin, and Jones, who had charge of the decorations. On tables around the room a number of curios, kindly lent by various friendq, were exhibited. A particu- larly fine collection of Indian and Burmese curios were lent by Mr. Fred Sandall, a moss stone, in which the growing moss was plainly visible, attract- ing a great deal of attention. Mr. Peers also tent a book printed on paper made from bamboo, illustra- tive of some of the uses to which bamboo is put in Jtlpan. Commencing at 7.30 p.m., a programme consisting of glees, songs, recitations, violin and clarionet solos, duets, &c., was gone through in a most able manner, and did not fail to meet with the appreciation it deserved, the accompanist beinz Miss- Mabel Garnett. The chair was occupied by the. president, Mr. T. Gandy. At the conclusion of the programme, refreshments, prepared by Mrs. T. Gandy, Miss A. Moses, and Miss Mabel Garnett, were handed round. After the refreshments the room was cleared, and a variety of games were in- dulged in and greatly enjoyed by everyone. At eleven o'clock the proceedings were brought to a termination by the singing of the National Anthem
BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A YOUTH. Thomas Shawcross, had been summoned for commit- ting a violent assault upon Peter Daley, a youth, at a lodging-house in Scotland-road, on the. 11th of December, but did not appear.—Mr. Brown, solicitor, who appeared for the complainant, and reminded the Bench that the case ha i stood over on account of the complainant hav- ing been in the infirmary.--The prosecutor said on the night in question he was asleep in bed with his brother Frederick at their father's house on the night of Decem- ber 11th, and was woke by the defendant striking him with his fist, the defendant hit him across the head with something iron. Witness went downstairs bleeding very much, and he was taken to the Infirmary. The doctor told him that his wound was over tyk inches long.—On the application of Mr. Brown a warrant was granted for the apprehension of Shawcross. UNCLEAN CANAL BOATS.—BoId Aldred, of Stamford- , road, Altrincham, and John Roughley, Salford, were summoned on Tuesday, before the magistrates of Dares- bury, for, having on the 4th December at Grappen- hall, contravened a regulation made by the Local Government Board, by allowing tho cabin of a boat to be in a dirty and defective condition.—The facts of the case were stated by Mr. Frank Kerfoot,inspector for the War- rington Rural Sanitary Authority.—Mr. Aldred who is the agent for the sale of manure for the Manchester Cor- poration, proved that he was neither owner nor agent, and the case against him was, therefore, dismissed.— Mr. Kerfoot said he should now summon Mrs. Pendle- bury, who, Mr. Aldred said, was the actual owner. The defendant Aldred then withdrew his plea of not guilty. He said he had written cheques for Mrs. Pendlebury, who was a relative of his, but he was not a paid agent Mrs. Pendlebury was now lying dangerously ill, and he would for the time being acknowledge himself as her. agent, so that she might not be troubled and annoyed with a summons. The evidence of the Inspector was then repeated, after which Mr. Aldred contended that Mrs. Pendlebury had been summoned under the wrong section.—The Magistrates' Clerk held that the objection was good, and the case against Mr. Aldred was dis- missed. The captain of the boat, Roughley. who had been summoned under another section, was fined ss. and costs.

AGGItAVATED ASSAULT ON A WOMAN. Edward Tynans, labourer, was charged with commit- ting an aggravated assault on Ellen Deloose, a married woman, living in Cheshire Cheese Yard, Winwick-st. The prosecutrix deposed: About seven o'clock On the evening of New Years's Day she was lying on the sofa, when the prisoner opened the house door and walked in. She asked him what he wanted, and he replied" No- thing." She told him his place was outside, and he thereupon seized her by the hair and dashed her on the floor. He then got hold of her by the legs, and she struggled to get free, and presently she got her hand free and hit him on the nose. She eventually got loose, and assumed the offensive, and he ran out. She pursued him, and meeting her husband gave him a description of the prisoner. Mr. Delooze subse- quently met a man answering his wife's description in Horsemarket-St., and accosted him. A struggle ensued, when P.C. Turner intervened, and ended it. Another witness was called and said he saw a man answering the description of the prisoner standing outside the prosecu- tor's house. P.C. Turner said Mrs.Deloose informed him •of the assault, and said the man had a mark on his nose where she had struck him. On taking him to the Police Station witness found a severe cut on the bridge of his nose. He denied the charge. The prisoner said the evi- dence against him was utterly untrue. He came from Bolton, where he worked for the London and North- Western Railway Co., in order to get a form filled in,and signed by a magistrate and went into the Crow Inn, 'Bridge-St., and afterwards was apprehended on this charge, but bad never been near the woman's house.— The prosecutrix recalled, said she was quite certain the prisoner was the man.—The prisoner in reply to the bench said he could not account for the cut on his nose, except by supposing that he must have got it in the struggle with the complainant's husband.—The Bench considered that there was a doubt in the case and dis- missed the prisoner, though informirag him that he had had a narrow escape. CATTLE DEALERS FINED AT DARESBURY. At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. Edward Greenall (in the chair), James Marson, and H. Nield, Messrs. William Bennett Bros. of Padgate, were summoned for causing two cows to be moved into a pleuro-pneumonia infected area without having a license authorizing them so to do. The offence was com- mitted at Stretton, on the 20th November.—Thomas Shakeshaft, in the employ of Messrs. Bennett, was charged with driving the animals into the infected area. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the defence.— Constable Bratt and other officers stated the facts of the case, but Brett said that on the day in question lie was on duty at Stretton when Shakeshaft brought the cows into the infected area. The man produced a veterinary surgeon's •certificate, but he had no license entitling him to remove the cattle. He had only a declaration that the animals were free from disease.—By Mr. Longton: The declara- tion was not sufficient. The cattle were only 30 or 40 yards wthin the infected area. Mr. Longton said Messrs. Bennett Bros. were highly respectable cattle dealers, and they were anxious to support the law and the magis- trates. On this occasion Mr. Walter Bennett had bought two cows at Chester, where no order with reference to the removal of cattle was in force, but he obtained a declaration to the effect that the animals were free from disease. They were taken to Norton Station. Mr. Bennett had called at the County Police Office at Chester to ask for a license to enable him to remove the cattle ' into an infected area, but it was.refused. He was told he must get one from the police-sergeant of the district into which the cattle were to be removed. The weather was cold, and all this time the cattle remained at Norton Station Mr. Bennett sent his man Shake-shaft to Sergeant Booth at Stockton Heath for a license, but the sergeant was from home, and he could not get it. Another messenger was sent later on. Mr. Shakeshaft went to Mr. Bennett at War- rington. who said, "These cows will die if they remain at the station. Move them slowly along the road towards Stretton, and I will send someone else to Sergeant Booth for the license, and will meet you at Stretton." A boy was sent to Sergeant Booth's house, but the sergeant was again from home. The officer in charge, however, said to the boy "We cannot attend to you, but don't take the cattle beyond the Cat and Lion, and then he will be all right." The lad went on to the Cat and Lion, bui; as the weather was cold he sheltered in the public-house, and whiM lie was doing so the cattle went by into the infected area. A fine of 40s. and costs was inflicted up- on Messrs. Bennett. The case against their man was dismissed on payment of the costs.—Mr. Bennett said he thought the sentence was a very severe one under the circumstances.

word of one man? The other says he did not see me do anything.—Aldennan Sutton: He saw you walking about in a very suspicious manner. AFFILIATION ARREARS.—James Higgins, canal worker, was apprehended under a warrant charged by Margaret Flannigan, with non-payment of £3 6s. arream in bastardy. He was ordered to pay, or go to prison for a month's hard labour. AN UNMUZZLED Doo.—John Gandy for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled in Lord Nelson-st., on the 9th inst., was ordered to pay 3s. 6d. costs. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Witham Wheeler, of Low Wash, was fined is. for having his chimney on fire on the 18th inst. FRIDAY. —Before Messrs. J. White and J. H. Gornall. DRUNK.—John Green, drunk on Now Year's night in King-st., was fined ss. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Jane Waterworth, who now made her 11th appearance, was committed for a month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., on New Year's night. ASSAULTING A WlFE.—Michael O'Neill. aged 26, was prosecuted by his wife Catherine C'Neill for assaulting her, and at her request was allowed the option of teing bound over in his own recognizances of £5 and a surety of £5 for his keeping the peace for six months, in de- fault a months' imprisonment. WIFE DESERTION.—Joseph Boardman, was charged with deserting his wife Margaret Boardman, a small shopkeeper. on the 13th inst. The defendant was her fourth husband.—Mr. Browne appeared for him, and said he bore an excellent character from his employers. The complainant admitted that when he left her it was on her ordering him out of the house.—The case was dismissed.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenell (in the chair), James Matson and H. Neild. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF CATTLR.I.TaIDOS MOYOtOII, farmer, Hatton, was summoned for having on the 27th November, at Walton, in contravention of an order made on the 25th July, under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, removed a cow through a pleuro-pneumonia infected area without having a license .authorizing him so to do. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.—Thomas Clough, butcher, Runcorn, and William Wormll. his servant,were summoned for a similar offence on the 15th December at Walton. The Chairman said that as the defendant was a butcher he should be familiar with the contents of the various orders, and he would be fined in a heavier penalty, namely, 20s. and costs.—William Nixon, farmer; Halton, and Chas. Houghton, labourer, were summoned for a similar offence, committed on the 22nd December. Nixon, the master, was fined 15s. and eosts-ss. for each animal removed. The case against Houghton, the servant, was dismissed on payment of thecosts. TUE REMOVAL OF CArrug.—Mr. Superintendent Large informed the Bench that the townships of Walton, I Grappenhall, and Appleton were now dissolved as cattle I infected areas. GAME TITESPASS.—A labourer named Frederick Cliffe , was summoned for having on the 7th December, at Whitley, committed a trespass by entering in the day- time on land in the possession and occupation of Thomas Hewitt, farmer, in search of conies, withouta license.- -The defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s. and costs. Mr. Hewitt did not press the case.. THE EDUCATION ACT.—Edward Goodier, Appleton, summoned for having on the 28th November, at Apple- ton, neglected to send his daughter Lillie to school, was fined ss.—Charles Delooze, of Walton. was summoned for a similar offence with respect to his son Charles Wil- fred, and an order was made upon the father to cause L his son to attend school at Stockton Heath. CRUELTY TO A HORSH.—Lousia Jane Burton was sum- moned for having on the 11th November, at Preston Brook, abused and illtreated a horse by working it while in an unfit state. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. DRUNKENNESS .—John Doyle, labourer, Grappenhall, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk at Grappenhall on the 15th ult.—Thomas Garvin, cab driver, Warring- ton, was summoned for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cab at Walton on the 30th of November. Constable Shatwell found the defendant asleep on his box opposite the Walton Arms Inn, at midnight on the 30th November. He with some difficulty he awoke the defendant, who was drunk. Witness got on the box and. drove to Warrington to Mr. Connor to whom the cab belonged. Defendant who admitted being asleep, was fined ss. and costs.—George Young, blacksmith, Little. Legh, was summoned for having on the 7th December- been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Adpleton, and was fined ss. and costs. HIGHWAY OFFENcEs.—John Horton, farmer, Little Legh, charged with allowing a horse to stray on the highway at Little Legh, on the 20th November, was fined Is. and costs.—Robert Spann, a labourer, was sum- atoned for an offence committed on the highway on the 28th November, at Preston-o'th-Hill. The officer who proved the case said the defendant was the driver of two horses and carts; but the horse of the hinder cart was not attached by a rein to the back of the first cart. The defendant was fined in the costs, 3s. 6d. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the charr), Councillor Voisey, and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNKENNESS. —Thomas Glavin, for being drunk and disoederly in Bank-st.' on Friday morning, was fined ss. and costs, or seven days.—Sergeant Jones proved the ease. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—A. number of persons- were summoned for neglect of maintenance orders levied on them by the borough magistrates Lloyd was ordered to pay 3s. 6d. a week to the support of his son on the ship Clio until the arrears, £4 10s. 6d., are paid ; Benjamin Ogden, whose arrears for his son on the same vessel are £2 2s. 6d., was ordered to pay 25. 6d. per week.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Gossage and Mr.. Brock. BEGOING.—Luke Darwell, a tramp, was sehtenced to , seven days' hard labour for begging. SLEEPING OUT.—For sleeping in Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.'s chemical works, on the previous evening,Thos. Booth and John Dagnall, tramps, were each sent to prison for seven days. TRAINED TO STEAL.—Jane Cain and her boy William, of 5, Martley-st., were charged with stealing.2icwts. of coal, from West Bank Dock, the property of the trustees of the late John Hutchinson. The prisoners were caught in the act by the watchman, Richard Hughes, the mother stating the boy acted under her directions,—Mrs. Cain was fined 205., and the boy was discharged. THEFT FROM A PUBLIC-11013SE.—Fred Gandy (14), of 3, West Bank-st., was charged with stealing two spirit glasses from the West Bank Hotel,the property of Messrs. Peter Walker and Co., Limited, on Christmas Eve. P.C. Davieson saw the prisoner leave the hotel, and noticing that his coat pockets were bulky, he searched him and 1 found the glasses. The prisoner was ordered to receive 1 six strokes with the birch rod. .

div.head: WAR RINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WAR RINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

A meeting of 4his Council will be held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The following ammg other business will be considered. ) THE Wearn COMMITTEE.—This Committee will recom- meat that Councillor Heaton be appointed a member of the Watch •Committee in the place of Mr. Tinsley, re- , signed ; and, that the Mayer, and Aldermen Chandley, iHarrison and Platt be appointed a sub-committee to consider the question of the pay and promotion of the police force.

NEW MEMBERS OF CommtrrEn.—The finance Commit- tee has appointed Councillor Monks a member of the Committee in the place of Mr. W. Tinsley. Mr. Monks has also been appointed a member of the Streets Improve- ment Committee in place of Mr. Dixon,who has resigued.. Councillor Fleming having resigned his position on the Cemetery Committee, Mr. Hill has been appointed to. succeed him. Mr. Hill has also been appointed a mem- ber of the Markets Committee. Another change on the Markets Committee is the substitution of Councillor Jenkins for Councillor Browne,the latter having resigned Councillor Greening has been appointed to the Gas Com- mittee in place of Mr. Tinsley. THE LIBRARY RATE.—The Finance Committee having being requested by the Museum, Library, and Arts Com- mittee to increase the provision for that Committee, according to the recent Improvement Act, to an amount equal to a rate of three half-pence in the £, it (the Finance Committee) has passed the following resolution "That when the estimates for the year 1891-2 -are made, the extra provision be brought into account." THE PROPOSED NEW BRIDGE AT WeuroN.--The Rivers , Committee reports that the following gentlemen met the Committee in conference on the plans submitted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, with respect to the proposed new bridge over the river at Walton, and the levels of the new roads viz. :—From the Warrington District Highway Board—Mr. J. Thompson, surveyor; from the Daresbury Highway Board—Messrs, Wm. Long, Thos. Hall, Darbishire, Jones, Peswick,and Swinton,sur- veyor ; from the Chamber of Commerce and traders of Warrington—Messrs. Jno. Fairclough and Robt. Garnett., The following resolution was unanimously passed and ordered to be sent to Mr. Leader Williams —"At: a nieeting of representatives of the Corporation of War- rington, the Warrington District Highway Board, the Daresbury Highway Board, and the Traders of Warring- ton, the following recommendations were unanimously agreed to :—That the new bridge to be constructed by the Manchester Ship Canal Company over the river at Walton, should be a fixed bride, having a headway equal to that of the London and North-Western Railway Company's bridge at Walton Arches, and that the Com- pany be requested to submit to the several Authorities interested a plan showing the levels of the new roads as. altered by this recommendation."

THE INTIMICEPTING DEPOTS.—Councillor Dixon has again placed on the agenda paper a motion to the effect that immediate steps be taken for closing the intercepting depots, either by the Sanitary Committee or by a speciale committee appointed by the Council.

Wicock was referee. WARRINGTON "A" V. LANCASTER "A return fixture between these teams was played on Saturday on the Wilderspool enclosure. Both fifteen had the assist- ance of several first team men,and at the time of starting a moderate number of spectators had assembled. War- rington started towards the pavilion goal, but Boscow immediately afterwards had to save a rush at his own quarter flag. Following a quick piece of play by Massey, a• rush in which Barnes, Teare, Turner, and Molyneux were notable, carried the ball towards the Lancaster lines. The stay, however, was of short duration ; for a magnificent fast run by Hartley, who was only stopped by Boscow when extremely dangerous, again enabled his side to attack strongly. Barnes relieved finely, and passing over to. Daniels, neutral territory was reached. • Some very fast and exciting play between the rival backs• was then witnessed, which ended in Rowe getting splen- didly away. This was quickly followed by a grand rush of the visitors, headed by Punchard, " 31rGinty," and Ralph, which carried play to the other end of the field, and a try was obtained by the former. After the drop out some powerful kicking by the visiting backs was of immense advantage, and constantly troubled the home defenders. A fine pass from Massey was then mulled, but Randles, Donohue. Mather, and Povey dribbled away to their opponents' quarters, and a grand piece of play by Mather, Rowe, and Davies took the leather to the limes.. As quickly the ball was taken to the home lines, when Mather brought about a slight relief. Smart play by Massey followed, but when half time arrived the score was unaltered. Restarting, Isherwood, Molyneux, Teare,.and Donohue rushed down the field, only to find a barrier in Cowell, who kicked back with interest. A lot of exciting play between both sets of forwards roused the enthusiasm of the spectators, and a groan of disap- poinment arose when a fine chance was missed from a long pass by Randles. A couple of kicks by Boscow and Massey took the scene of warfare to the Lancaster lines, when, after a few anxious moments, the visitors relieved in a body, and tackled Boscow in his own quarters. ' Chiefly by the instrumentality of Donohue and Boscow, play was located at the centre line, and from this point a remarkable change came over the. game.. Up to this stage Lancaster had played splendidly, but now fell away, whilst the homesters improved wonderfully. Povey was the first to score, and the cheers had barely swbsided when Turner secured another. After some capital 'play by leare, Povey, and Molyneux, and a fine run by Rowe, a try was secured by Randles from a dribble headed by Turner, Davies, and Barnes, and the point was im- proved by Davies. Soon after the kick off a grand dribble by Turner was the next item, when Barnes made a brilliant dodgy run and pass to Mather, who threw wide to Daniels, the latter running over in fine style.and the result of a splendidly-contested game was: War- rington 1-4-2 to 0-1-0. Lancaster: Full back, Clarke; three-quarter backs, Hartley, Cowell, and Goodman ; half backs, Danby and Gardiner; forwards, Jones, " MiGinty,” Barber, Ralph, Punchard, Watson, Pinch, Lofthouse, and Stephenson.

ATTEMPTING TO ENTER LOCK-UP Snop.—Reginale Gascoyne,was charged with attempting to break into the lock-up shop of John Cross, butcheron Golden Square, on Sunday morning. P.C. Bowen deposed that about half- past ten a.m , on the 28th, be received information that a man had been attempting to enter the shop. Witness while going down Horsemarket-st. met Thomas Wright who pointed out to him the prisoner as being the nlan who had attempted the depredation and said lie (Wright) had released him from a hook by which he had got fast in trying to get down from the window. Witness examined the premises and found dirt on the window sill and also on the hook. There was a hole in the pri- soner's coat which corresponded with the hook. The windows of the premises were always left open, so that by getting on to the window ledge and reaching up to the top of the sash admission could easily be obtained. The prisoner led witness to suppose that he belonged to America, and had only reached England on the 18th. He came from Manchester on Sunday night.—Thomas Wright said about five minutes to ten on Sunday morn- ing he saw the prisoner on the ledge of the lock-up shop and trying to get down. He had got fast by his boot and his coat to a hook. Witness released him, and he got down and went away, and half an hour after wit- nesssaw him again.—William WriLtht said he saw the prisoner walking round near the shoo at five minutes ta nine and for abo. ut half an hour afterwards. The police officer asked witness whether he had seen such a man knocking about, and witness said he had, and pointed out the prisoner.—The prisonerdenied his guilt, and said he knew nothing about the matter. If he had wanted to break into any butcher's shop lie had sufficient oppor- ' tunity during the night, as he was in the town all night. --He was committed to prison for a month.—The pri- soner: Is that man's word to be taken against mine, the
THE ESSEX MURDER.-INQUEST AND
VERDICT.

The inquest on the body of Joseph Leatherdale, farmer, of Salcot, Essex, whose body was discovered in a cup- board at his farmhouse, and whose nephew is in custody on suspicion of having caused his death, was concluded on Tuesday at Salcot. Evidence" was given by Mrs. Sortwell, daughter of the deceased, as to contradictory statements made by the accused after the disappearance of her father. Dr. James, who had made a post-mortem examination, stated that death was caused by a gunshot wound at the base of the skull. Mrs. Conly, a neigh- bour, deposed that on Saturday morning, December 20, she arranged with the deceased to go in his trap to Col- chester. About an hour afterwards the accused called for her, and said his uncle tiad gone to Kelveston. Some little time previously witness heard the muffled report of a gun. Other neighbours testified as to the accused being in possession of a considerable amount of money after the disappearance of his uncle, Mr. Jones, clerk to the county magistrates, produced a written statement signed by the prisoner to the following effect :—" I did not kill my uncle, but got someone to do it. I told him all the money he had in his pocket he should have for the job, and he got some more to help him, and after they had shot him I gave them a sack and a halter. This is all I have got to say, and I shall not split."—Police Sergeant Creasy proved having found on the prisoner's clothing stains of blood. The accused told him that his uncle grumbled at him, kept him at work all day, and gave him only is. 6d. a week.—The Coroner having summed up, the jury returned a verdict of wilful mur- der against the accused, Arthur Leatherdale.

Eterton, on the other hand, had a vastly different ex-1 perience, as .they triumphed over Motherwell,Accrington,,t and lihrnlci. Mr.'llhomas Richards, member of Parliament for the HartlepoolS, died suddenly on Monday at hi-/'resideace, Kirklevington, near Yarm, Yorkshire, at the age of 69; from the.effects of a chill. div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
MORE ICE ACCIDENTS.
THE SEVERE WEARER.

Snow fell slightly in the metropolis:on Tuesday night, and there was twelve degrees of. frost._ A man was over- come by the intense cold at the East Ham Railway 'Sta. tion, Essex, on Wednesday morning, and expired/from failure to the heart. A tramp was, found in a ditth aro i Barking, on Wednesday morning, frozen and insensible. HE was removed to the lafirmary. A snowstorm df great severity commenced at. Queenstown at midnight,, on Tuesday night, and tl.o Thite Star steamer Majestic and the Allan steamer Polynesian, front Halifax and St. John's, which arrived off , ths harbour, were unable to communicate with the shore, and proceeded to Liver- pool without landing passengers or. mails. Owing to the severe frost, there ,was skating on the Thames on,Wed- nescla.y, at Windsor: This is the first time ice has, been sufficiently strong to allow skating there since- 1355 when a alcket match was played on the ice.

such objects. We read of .strikes and ot ead feeling between employers and employed, and we knew of the unhappiness created by these, and he heartily deplored their existence. But occasions like the present promoted good feeling betv'eeem the two classes, as showing how much those in influential positions thought of the class to which their employes belonged. He exhorted the women present to use their power as wives and mothers to favourably influence their husbands rend sons. There were, he said, many excellent qualities, he had reason to know, in Warrington. He had received so much kindness in it from all classes that it made him most aNIXiOUS for the future welfare of its boys and girls. • (Applause.) Mr. T. MORRIS then made a financial statement as treasurer of the fund. He said before. they started col- lecting for the treats they had £4O in the bank. The treats would cost something like £BO, and if he did not get thiehe would have to draw some ofthe £VO. He did not want to.do that, but he wished to add to it, so as to have a reserve fund to provide the treat without going to their friends for subscriptions. Fouror five years ago this wee the case, but to relieve the distress then exist- ing in Warrington the Committee, in the goodness of their hearts spent the amount, -and also nearly all they had in the bank. Mr: Morris, amidst much applause, described the gift of Mr. Fletcher as a noble one, remarking that the tea and sugar supplied by him would cost about £2O. He pointed out that the committee preferred not to have a few large sums for the animal treats, but many small sums e as this would show that the town generally subscribed. He concluded by calling for hearty claps for the subscribers to the treats ; and the-appeal was promptly responded to. Alderman Witione having made a few observations, an entertainment followed, in which- the- artistes were • Mr. Gr. Gemson, of Liverpool; Mr i G. Riley (the accone- - paniit), Mr. S. Sutton, Mr. Paul Conway, Mr. Furness, wheobtained an encore, Miss Fanshaw, who received an encore for one of her performances. Miss F. Jones, Mr. Hairy Collin, comic singer and impersonator, who was - deeidedly the favourite of the evening,, and received a vbeiferous encore on each of his-appearances. During the interval between the two parts the tea and sugar eeere distributed; and something- or other occurred in Onnection with this part of the proceedings which occa- sioned great merriment. i At the close of the concert Alderman Wright called for three hearty cheers for the ladies and gentlemen who had so kindly given their services during the evening; and enthusiastic cheers were given. Subsequently mince pies were distributed, and all presentthen dispersed to their homes. ANOTHER TREAT FOR THE 'AGED :IND POOR. On Monday evening in connection with the mission work being carried on in Warrine.:,ton by Mr. Joseph Wibberley, of the Independent Methodistsea free tea and ' supper were provided in the Brick-st. Sunday School. There was -a large gathering of • deservingepeople, who were provided with a substantial meat tea at, the expense Mr. J. Hamblen, of Winwick-read; The treat was tended to take the place of a gift of bread which Mr. Hamblett—along with a supply of coal—has generously • distributed among the deserving poor during the winter months. The tea having been partaken Mr. James Evans took the chair, and a very interesting entertain- - ment was-given by the members of the Stinday School. In the course of a short address Mr. Wibberley gave an account of his recent mission work, expressing his sin- cere-thanks to the many friends who had 'assisted him by-their gifts of left-off clothing, etc., especially to Mr. Hamblen whose gifts to the poor had been many and varied and through whose -kindness they were met - together. Mr. Sambrooks followed. and expressed the • pleasure it gave him to see such a happy assembly. The entertainment which followed gave great satisfaction, and pleasure. A musical sketch, "Have your own way,' was listened to with interest, -the characters being sus, tamed by Misses Warburton, and Braenhall and Mr. R. Hatledine. The Lancashire sketches of Mr. C. Furness,' - as usual; caused much merriment, as also-did the efforts of Messrs. Hazledine and N. Cook in the songs "TM Cork Leg" and "Grandmother's Chair."- At the close of the programme a hearty vote of -thanks to Mr. Ham- blett was passed with loud applause. The quartette, • "Good- 'Night," having been sung, supper-was served to all present. and after the presentation-of a mince pie to ' alethe guests—some 140 in -number—thseneeting term'- • nated. It was announced at the close of the gathering that ate-in former years the gift of coal would be made ' to all present, and that 1 cwt. would be delivered at the new year. The doxology having been sung, the party separated amid mutual expressions of thunklulness and t emoyment. We understand that since the meeting, severah anonymous gifts have been received by Mr: Wibberley at his residence, 26, Battersby-lane.and whilst expressing their thanks for this timely h&p,. the workers • would' remind the public that the work is carried on solely by voluntary subscriptions 4 and that any gift will be-thankfully received.

div.head: ANNUAL TREATS TO AGED MEN AND WOMEN.
div.p: ANNUAL TREATS TO AGED MEN AND WOMEN.

The annual treats given.tby public subscription, to the poor aged men and women of Warrington, came off in the Public Hall, on New Year's Day. About 12 o'clock between 300 and 400 old men, of 60 years of age and upwards sat down to a most .substantial and excellently cooked dinner, consist- ing of beef, mutton, pork, rabbit pie, and plum pudding„accompanied with beer, that is, where beer Lwas prefei/ed to a present of tobacco which was L:given inter on to those who chose it. The Committee on whemdevolved the duty of making the neces- sary preparations, and seeing to the proper dispen- sation of the creature comforts to the aged people, consisted) of the following gentlemen ;—Alderman Sutton, president; Mr. Thomas Jones, vice-presi- dent; Alderman Wright, secretary; Mr. T. Morris, treasurer; and Messrs. P. Chrimes, C. Skinner, S. Jones.G PlUing, Fanshaw, D. Jones, and P. Cald- wellrall these gentlemen being present. Among others present, many of whom constituted them- , selves ready auxiliaries in serving out the viands, , were:—The Mayor (Alderman Francorah), Alder- • rr.an Holmes, the Rev. F. W. Willis (rector), and • Mrs. Willis, the Rev._E. C. Carleton, and Mrs. Carle- . ____ _

ton, the,Rev. H. Buckton, the Rev. F. C. Timins, the Rev. Thomas Ross, Messrs. J. Smethurst, I. Hay- ward, X.. Hayward, H. Toft, B. P. Stringer, and G. Riley, and Dr. Peacocke. About forty persons were present in the galleries to witness the proceedings; and the sight of the numorous tables—one of

which had to be placed on the platform—crowded with aged men whose faces expressed the con- sciousness that for a brief time, at any rate, their lives had fallen in pleasant places, and who were all showing in the most practical form, appre- ciation of the good things provided for them, was a most pleasing one. Music, which is said to be pro- motive of good digestion, was not absent as a con- comitant to the feast, for Mr. W. S. Woods, organist ofthe.Phrish Church, sent forth sonorous strains from the hall organ, albeit some might consider that the solemn tones of such an instrument,. were li little too heavy for the occasion. Grace we oughi to mention was said by the Rev. F. W. 'Willis, the organ expressing the same petition immediatell after in music. At the close of the repast, Alderman SUTTON proposed the health of Her MajeslY the Qbeen, which was drunk with three cheers. Alder- man Sutton then said he had on behalf of the Committee to give the' guests a hearty welcome and to wish ever.? one ofthent a very happy and prosperous New year. He then read a statement showing that the ages of those who had, dined there that day ranged from 60 to 89, the mention of this age as that of the oldest guest prOent, being received with applause. The next oldest masi. was was one of 811. he being the only one rejoicing in thst age, two ethers of 82 coming next to him. The total /limber of old tnementertained to dinner, he stated, was 00., and he hoped and believed they had all laJoYed it. Some of his friends had said how vet' nice it was All he could say was that if it was not nice it ought to be, because the' Commiltee had been very particular indeed in procuring the Iry best meat they could buy in the town, and all the her ppro- visions. were of the very best. Among the aPPlicants for tickets; there had been a great many men st under 60 years of age. The Committee were very sorri to refuse, t thervilentthey eeuld only accomodate a containhis number, not more • than the 360 present. Of course winter was an exceptionally severe one, but at thesame time he was-told that a great many of these rking-men 'who hadmot arrived at 60 years of age did tot act up to the sensible advice of making hay while the sun shone. He knew fora fact that unfortunately many f orking-men who were offeredwork di d not takeadvantagof the oppor- e -tunityoNvorking when they had the chance' to do it; and , many.. instead efi working six full days b Week, when they could have-the privilege of doing thy could not be got to-work morethan four or five. Now, if they would take the opportunity of working the wheiesix days they could: put by a little to provide for therraelvea on these lestiveperiods, and at those times whentheY were un- able towork on account of the severe weather. He hoped the present weather would soon pass away and that everyone would have full work atm, and go on prosperously for the new year. (Applaase,) The Rev. F. W. Virtrars expressed ci, behalf of the guests their sincere gratitude to the Cefuniittee for their effeets that day:. Hie would mention tFewrepresentative names, than which he did not think tree better could be picked out, M. Sutton, president, hIr..F. E. Wright, treasurer, and' Mr. Thomas Morris, iecretary. div.head: " KOCH COMES IMMEDIATELY."
div.p: " KOCH COMES IMMEDIATELY."

A little while ago the resident doctor of the little Polish town taf Pabiania received a telegram from Berlin, With the following significant words, "Koch comes im- mediately." No sooner had the young telegraph official Spelt out these words than he left his office to take care of itself, and hurried like lightning from house to house to inform his friends and acquaintances of the gieat Piece of news that Robert Koch would appear in Pabiania. This news spread like wildfire through the town and met With all the more credence as it was known that Count ' who resided in a splendid castle near Pabiani3, was suffering from a weak chest, and had interestO himself greatly in Koch's discovery. It was inferred that Count P., through the meditation of the Pabiania Physician, had invited Professor Koch to attend him. The clever people of Pabiania considered it a duty and an honour to give the great German man of science a l worthy reception. At a meeting promptly held in one of the best restaurants in the place it was solemnly resolved to receive him at the entrance of , the town and to invite him to a splendid banquet. The , sPeeeh ef welcome, in the temporary absence of the Physician, was entrurted to the apothecary of the town I for delivery in French, or, if necessary, Latin. The ,great day arrived. In swallowtails and white ties, their fur coats thrown lightly over their shoulders, the town digni- taries, under the leadership of the Burgomaster, waited Oil the highroad for the arrival of the coach which was to bring the great man from the next railway station. At one o'clock the carriage came in sight, and in it a man With a German fur coat. The apcthecary, who had gained the necessary courage by drinking several glasses of home-made brandy, stepped courageously forward, cleared his throat, and began " H'm, monsieur, j'ai Phonneur de vous dire joli bonjour ! H'm, h'm, mon- sieur! Dominus lupum vincit ! Lupus non es in futuro I" " Merci inerci ! merci !" echoed all the quality of Pabiania. Meanwhile the stranger, much frightened, drew his passport out of his pocket, and holding it under gle apothecary's nose, made it plain that the new arrival was a new cook from Berlin engaged by Count P.! The notabilities crept home ashamed; each one laid the blame on the other, but the telegraph official suffered most. " Roth " means in German "cook," and the telegraphist had jumped to erroneous conclusions.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- !tan Harrison presided, and there were also present the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, and G. F. Roberts; Messrs. Ratcliffe, Blackhurst, Balharry, Dobson. J. Houghton, Kilshall, Swinton, Turton, W. Hough ton, Hood-Wright, Clarke, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sut- ton (assistant-clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse mas- ter), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools).

THE CHRISTMAS DINNER. The Workhouse Master reported that the Christmas dinner passed off satisfactorily, the inmates conducting themselves in an exemplary manner. The CHAIRMAN expressed satisfaction with this report, and stated that he had himself been prevented from being at the Work- house on Christmas Day through the slipperiness of the grouad.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he was also prevented from attending by a bad cold.
VACCINATION AT PENHETH.

The Local Gov—er-n-m—e-n-t—go;;d-ZOTe.; the effect that their vaccination inspector, Mr. Thompson, had recently 'visited this district and from his report it appeared that there were very few vaccinations performed at the Pen- Iteth stationionly 13 children having been vacinated there la the first three quarters of this year. It was therefore 89ggested that it would be sufficient if attendances were given at the station every three consecutive weeks at half-yearly periods, say in April and October, instead of • quarterly periods as at present.—The CLERIC said the ex- Planation for that was the fact that the people of Pen- as a rule engaged their own doctors to vaccinate their children.—lt was decided by the Board to adopt the suggestion of the Local Government Board.

div.head: CHAPLAINCY QUESTION.
div.p: THE CHAPLAINCY QUESTION.

In the minutes of a previous meeting of the Board Whilst in committee it was stated that it had been Solved to advertise for a chaplain for the workhouse at eso a year, and to pay Father Feeny, of St. Alban's Roman Catholic Church, £lO a year for his spiritual ministrations to the Catholic inmates.—The CLERK read letter he had received from the Rev. J. J. Langham, vicar of Padgate, stating that he should be glad to act as chaplain to the Paugate Industrial Schools which were in his parish. It would be his desire to leave the question of remuneration entirely in the hands of the Guardians.—Mr. W. FIOUGHTON, in accordance with notice of motion, moved that Mr. Langham be appointed Chaplain of of Padp...ate schools at £lO a year.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLTON seconded this proposal, and, referring to the workhouse chaplaincy, he said he quite approved Of the proposal that £lO should be given to the Roman Catholic priest,but bethought it would be very unadvisable to take that sum from one religious body and give it to another. He was of opinion that anything that was given to the Catholic priest should be an additional charge on the Union.—Mr. BLACKHURST asked if the £lO a Year that was already paid to Padgate Church as pew rents went into the Vicar's pockets ?—Mr. W. HOUGHTON Said it did go as pew rents, but for that sum they had something like double value, as seats were found in the church for from 100 to 140 children from Padgate Schools, besides ten or a dozen officers.—Mr. BrAcxHunsT : Then )1()u mean to give the Vicar of Padgate £2O; I would rather you put it in that way. He did not see why they Should raise a stipend in that way, and then be so nig- gardly, with the Roman Catholic priests, to whom they ,Only proposed to give £lO, although it had been '''°'‘vn that they did a vast amount of work in Connection with that Workhouse. If they were going to be so liberal with the Church of England other people ?ught to be liberally dealt with. He thought there would 13e far more equity in proposing to give £2O to the Catholic priest at Warrington than in raising the salary latt Padgate.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON pointed out that the Catholic priest at Woolston was paid £lO a year for, Pew rents, jut.t as the Vicar of Padgate was, while Only about 40 children went to the Catholic Chapel and over 100 to Pa dgate Church. --Mr. BLACKHURST thought a clergyman's duty at the workhouse must be a great deal heavier than at Padgate Schools. Therewas scarcely ever a death at the Schools, while there were frequent ,deaths and funerals at the workhouse.—The Rev. C. B. CARLETON : You pay additional fees for lune- CHAIRMAN asked if the seats were free at augate Church.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said some were, but those occupied by the children from the schools were n°t•—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS proposed that instead of should £lO for pew rents and £lO for chaplain they "'"ould appoint the Vicar of Padgate as chaplain to the Schools with a salary of £29 a year. His feeling was that all churches should be free, and that at all times peo- Pie should be cordially invited.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the notice of motion could not be altered hi the Y suggested by Mr. Roberts.—Mr. ACKLAND said Mr. aogham had proferred to act as chaplain at the schools without any reinuneration.7—Mr. J. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the ormiges best suited for " " marmalade making are grown. A recent" "frost (the like of wh:ch has not been ex-" " perienced for ten years), has played havoc" "with the fruit, and, although though the 'S " full extent of the damage is not yet" " known, it is believed that fully one half " " the orange crop has been destroyed." " Luckily one shipment has been made to" " Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" " SS " Lurburan," which has just arrived." The Liverpool firm of W. H. div.p: tetttr to tin Otittar.
TOLSTOI AND CHRISTANITY
Sir,—Other matters having occupied my attention last week, I did not make any reply to Mr. Peer's letter of the previous week; but, with your permission, I will do so this week in a very few words. _

The concluding portion only of his letter was addressed to me, and to my surprise his only answer to my statements was a mere assumption. Ha fails to give a single text cr passage from the gospels which even implies the .necessity of a belief in the dogmas of the Fall and Redemption. Now I repeat most emphatically that 4Cluist never taught anything of the kind, and that no- where does he say anything that can reasonably warrant even an assumption for such a belief. I am well aware that these dogmas were taught by the apostles—notably by St. Paul ; and it has been said that St. Paul not Christ—was the founder of Christianity, Now, in the days of Christ, when his disciples were constantly with him, and had the benefit of hearing him daily, they con- tinually misunderstood him. He frequently chided and corrected them, but to so little purpose that after his death they thought all was over, and went about their daily work in just the same manner as before he called them. He had to appear to them again after the resur- rection before they took up his work and began to preach. And now comes the strangest part of it all. They were ignorant and unlearned men, and though, whilst Christ was living, they did not understand him and his teachings. yet, after his death, the letters they wrote to the various churches they had established were collected together and incorporated into Holy Writ. I, for one, must be excused if I decline to concede so much to them. I cannot allow them to be iniallible in any sense. I prefer to abide by the teachings of Christ himself. They surely are sufficient for man's salvation. The devices some people have to resort to to uphold some of these dogmas of Orthodox Christi?nity are sufficiently startling at titne.,. I have all my life be- longed to tte Wesleyan body, and one of our most dis- guisned ministers is the Rev. J. A. Eeet—Profe• ior Beet he is called. Some little time ago he delivered the Fernley Lecture—an annual event in our body—before the assembled conference. The subject of hll, lecture was" The Credentials of the Gospel." this lecture was published, and was put into my hands by an esteemed friend. Well, sir, I was very much struck with certain things in this lecture. It was an attempt to prove the gospels to be true and anthentic ; and by way of doing so the Rev. Professor makes the deliberate statement that they were not written by their reputed authors—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. He says they were written by anonymous writers at un- known dates—that, in fact, no one knows when, or where, or by whom they were written. And yet they are the Word of God. But he claimstliat the Epistles of St. Paul are genuine—that they were really written by St. Paul. I wish some of these writings of our church dignitaries were better known. I wish the general body of our people were better acquainted with the writings of Professor Beet, D. Dallinger, F. Ballard, and others. If they would only read and think, what a change we should see I Parts of Professor Beet's "credentials" are really very good, but other parts are utterly illogical and weak—so weak that I am amazed that he ever uttered them, much less published them. If I were sure that your readers were interested in this subject, I would tell them a few more startling things that have been written by eminent divines and others about the scriptures. Sir, the days of creeds and dogmas are hurrying to a close. In another generation or two they will excite the amazement and merriment of the world.—Yours, Sze., JOHN GANDY.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
REPORT OF PROGRESS.

The Directors announce that the cutting near Trafford Hall, at Barton, Stickens Island, Hulme Bridge, Davy- hulme, Irlam, and Latchford are now emptied and excavation has recommenced. Concrete work and masonry have since been pushed on with vigour, except when interfered with by the frost. The cutting at Partington is now being pumped out -and will be dry in about ten days; and at Pomona docks one portion has been cleared of water and excavation resumed, and the remainder will be emptied as soon as the frost is over. The masonry and concrete work at the various docks and locks have withstood the severe test in a most satisfactory manner as also have the completed portions of the slopes of the cuttings. The temporary bridges and railways damaged by the flood have now been restored. The brickworks at Thel- wall, which were flooded, and which are capable of pro- ducing upwards of 450,000 bricks per week, have aho been ready for work for some days past. As ail illustra- tion of the rate at which the pumping proceeded it may be stated that the Canal between Stickens Island and the Cheshire Lines Railway at Irlam, a length of 3 miles, was emptied at the rate of 2ft. in depth per day. The volume of water that passed down the river was consid- erably in excess of any flood which has occurred since the great one of 1866, and it is satisfactory to know that had it not been for the large works now in course of con- struction the effect of the floods would have approached the disaster of that year. The works between the en- trance locks at Eastham and the mouth of the river Weaver have been pushed forward day and night and great progress has been made, but owing to the abnor- mal rainfall in November and the recent severe weather it will not be possible to open that portion of the Canal until the spring of the year.
