THE ROSEBUDS' MISSION.

For a long time back it had been a daily occur- rem° for the men who worked on the dock from which the Stormy Petrel had once sailed, to be accosted by a sweet-fazed, poorly-clad woman hold- ing by the hand a little girl, and her question

always was: "Goo(1 men, has the ship come in yet? Have you seen my husband ?" And the men would answer kindly, and gaze after her with a pitying look upon their rough faces; and perhaps they would say in explanation

to a stranger : "Poor thing her husband was drowned with the Stormy Petrel, which went down six years ago, and since then she's lost her reason, and is all the time watching for the ship to come in." But one day they missed her usual visit, and after a while they heard that she had died, leav• ing two children motherless as well as fatherless. A month had passed since from their humble home their mother's cold form had been borne, and things were growing very hard for the

orphans. - Patience, the eldest, was a girl of sixteen, while her little sister was only seven. Though so young, for a long time Patience had been the bread-win- ner for their small family, going cheerfully to and from her work in the factory where she had found occupation. But within the last week the factory had been closed for want of sufficient money to carry it on. It was a cold day, and the chill wind and lower- ing sky made everything seem very dreary within the poor room where the orphans sat hand in hand. "Oh, Patience I" sobbed little Fannie, "I'm so hungry I Do you think God can be good as they say He is, to let a poor little girl starve who has never done any one any harm?' The elder sister laid her fingers gravely on the younger one's lips. "Hush, Fannie ! It is wrong to speak or even think like that." The child did not reply to her sister's reproof, but sat as if pondering something within her mind. All at ones she rose, and kneeling by their little bed, she clasped her hands. "Oh, God," she said, in her pathetic childish voice "please do not let us starve, but care of us Jesus's sake." As Patience heard, the bitter tears rolled down her young face. The girl had tried her best, but since she had been thrown out of employment, she had not been able to find anything to do. Every- thing of value they had possessed, from her mother's wedding ring down even to their clothes, she had disposed of; but now their money was all gone, and starvation stared them in the face. She rose and went to the window. It was noontime, and from all sides people were hurrying to and fro, and, notwithstanding the in- clemency of the weather, most of their faces were glad; for were they not going home? As Patience stood there, looking out, a delicate perfume attracted her attention. A sudden thought came to her. She had often seen chil- dren selling flowers in the street; might not she do the same, and earn some money, if only enough to keep the grim wolf from their threshold a little
longer. Before her, upon the window sill, stood two flower-pots, which held her most precious treasures. In one was a white rose•bush, while the other held

a sweet-scented geranium. It was not long before the three snowy buds, which wore all the plant bore, were clipped off, and together with a few geranium leaves, made into tiny bouquets; then wrapping around her her thin shawl, and kissing her little sister good by, Patience sallied forth. On the corner of a busy street she paused. Many glanced at the sweet, sad face of the young flower seller as they passed—some with pity, and some with indifference—but none stopped to buy the bouquets she held out to their notice. At length the afternoon was waning, and the cold was becoming more intense, and as yet the poor child had not met with any success. Tired and disheartened, she turned at last and walked with slow steps homeward. Bitter thoughts were surging through her young mind. To-morrow was the Sabbath —God's holy day. She had read in her Bible that not even a sparrow fell that the Heavenly Father did not know and heed; and yet He was going to let her little sister starve. Truly, it was hard to hold fast to her shield of Faith in the midst of such adversity. Just then a hand was laid on her shoulder, and a tall, grey-haired man, with a pleasant though bronzed and weather-beaten face, said: "You look cold, my lass." "Indeed I am very cold, sir," Patience an- swered; then, gathering her courage: " Don't you want to buy is flower ?" The eagerness of her tones, together with the sight of the tearful eyes and shivei ing, thinly-clad figure, went straight to the old sailor's heart. It was easy to see from Ms clothes and speech that he was a sea-faring iran. "To be sure I do. I love flowers. But first tell me what makes you look so sad? Perhaps it you do I can help you." The sympathetic tones broke down the girl's last remnant of fortitude, and won by the genuine kindliness of his face, she sobbed out her story. How, six years before, her dear father had sailed away, never to return. How from sorrow for Lis loss hor mother had lost her reason and had lately died, leaving her with her little sister all alone in the world. Then she told him of her struggle and failure to obtain em- ployment, and that for a whole day they had had nothing to eat—not even a crust of bread. As she spoke her listener g %vu a great start. " What's your name, lass?" he said, in husky tones. " Patieoce D.ll‘sorth," she replied, looking with wonder into his agitated face. With a cry, regardless of any who might be ob- serving him he caught her in his arms. "Little Patience !" he exclaimed. "My daughter found, thank God, at last 1" Patience gave one glance up into his face, and then she know that, though changed by the flight of years, it was indeed her father. That evening the humble room held hearts hap- pier than could be found in many a kingly palace, when, with little Fannie (who was a baby when he had last seen her) upon his knees, and Patience by his side, the old sailor told them how it was that he had been wrecked, bnt not lost, with the vessel as all had supposed; how he had been cast upon a desert island, whence he had been rescued three months ago, only to find the cottage home where he had left his wife and loved ones deserted, and to be told by the neighbours that they had, several years before, been obliged to go into the city to find work to maintain themselves; and that they had lately heard that his wife had died, though of the children's whereabouts they could tell him nothing. Since then he had sought far and wide for news of his lost daughters; but till now in vain. The morrow came, and found Patience and her sister in a cheerful, comfortable home, no longer fearing the future, but safe within the shelter of a father's protecting love. "Sister," said little Fannie, with a solemn earn- estness upon her childish face, "it was my prayer that did it. I know that God heard, for I asked him, 'for Jesus's sake,' and Jesus was once a little child like me." "We must never be parted again, my children," the old sailor said; and they never were, even when, a few years later, a young mechanic' with useful hands and an active brain, who bid fair in time to mount to the topmost round of the ladder of success which he had Just begun to climb, wooed and won gentle Patience to share his modest home. In Patience's soft brown hair, as she stood before the minister to be married, nestled a cluster of white rosebuds. They were plucked that morning with reverent lingers trom the bush which was the means of turning their sorrow into joy, and in little Fannie's mind is regarded with a love seldom bestowed upon an inanimate thing.

A LADY of the Far West, when she wants a cloak, yaps minx enough to get one in six months. A lady in Chicago, hearing this, began trapping, caught a single animal, and now has a cloak worth £5OO. It wasn't a quadruped she caught. THE hospitality of some people has no roof to it. Ten people will give you a dinner for one who will offer you a bed and a breakfast. George Macdonald.

Wednesday's report:from Hull states that the dockers' strike is increasing, several more vessels having been blocked. . Nearly the whole of the labourers at the Victoria Docks, London, struck work on Thursday morning, demanding to be paid for the dinner half-hour. They were promptly conducted out of the docks by the police. The strike 1 appears to have originated among a number of men who had been drafted into the Victoria Docks from what are called the up-town docks. where the labourers have been paid for meal time.

div.head: LTMAI.
div.p: LTMAI.

WESLEYAN BAND or HOPE.—The weekly meeting of the above society was held on Monday evening. There was a good attendance. Mr. Joseph Thorpe presided and de- livered a suitable address. The rest of the evening was spent in singing and reciting. ROSE IN THE VALLEY" DIVIDEND SOCIETY.—The annual audit of this society took place on Monday at the lodge room, Bull's Head Hotel, Lymm, when Mr. George H. Leigh produced his books for the year before Mr. Holt, Lymm, and Mr. Hewitt, of High Legh, the audi- tors. The books were found to be correct in every par- ticular. The dividend this year is the largest which has been declared for the past 23 years, the sick pay during the year having been light. No death has been recorded during the year. THE BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A con- cert in connection with this Society took place in the schoolroom on Wednesday evening. There was a large attendance of the members and their friends. Mr. Brundritt, president, occupied the chair. The pro- gramme was capitally r*ndered and highly appreciated. Those who took part were Mr. Jones,-Mr. Thomason ; Mr. Peters, Mr. Perkins, Mr. Gould, and Mr. Hall. A vote of thanks to the performers brought the concert to a close. WATCHNIGHT SERVICE AT LY3f3f .—The annual watch. night service was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Eagle-brow, on Wednesday night. Represen- tatives of the various dissenting denominations in the village were present and took part in the proceedings. The Rev. W. Evans conducted the service. Mr. Mercer (Independent Methodist) and the Rev. C. Clay (Congre- gational) gave suitable addresses. Mr. F. 0. Maton (Wesleyan) also took part in the proceedings. There was a large congregation present. The meeting separated a few minutes after the advent of the new year. "SHEPHERDS BY NIGHT "LODGE.—The audit of this society took place on Tuesday afternoon at their lodge room, Nag's Head Hotel, Lymm, when Mr. James Astley of Lymm, and Mr. G. H. Winstanley, of Beechwood, took the place•of Mr. A. Oliver, of Heaton Mersey, Man- chester, who could not attend, as auditors. Mr. George H. Leigh produced his books as secretary, and Mr. Robert Ditchfield, of Thelwall, as treasurer, both being congratulated on the way the books and vouchers had been kept. The Secretary pointed out another great saving to the lodge funds, as there had been so little paid for sickness during the year. CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT HIGH LEGH.—On Monday evening, a public meeting under the auspices of the Altrincham Division Conservative Association was held in the schoolroom, High Legh, in support of the Govern- ment. Colonel Cornwall Legh presided, and he was supported by Mr. Coningsby Disraeli (Conservative can- didate for the Altrincham division), Hon. J. E. Cross, Messrs. F. R. B. Lindsell, T. E. Walton, J. Worrall, H. Gibbon, A. Callender, r. Wright, T. Rigby, E. Swan- wick, &c.—The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said he had been asked to preside at the meeting that night, and he had much pleasure in doing so. It was some years since he had the pleasure of doing so, and he hoped if he lived he might be allowed to perform the same duty, and in so doing support the Unionist Govern- ment.—Mr. J. Worrell moved a resolution in favour of the Government, and Mr. H. Gibbon seconded.----Mr. Coningsby Disraeli supported the resolution, and was cordially received. He said he was very pleased indeed to be there, and to be able to address them,because although he had been to Lymm twice, and hoveringround, he had never been to High Legh to attack the electors in theirlair. The Hon. J. E. Cross proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Disraeli for his address. He hoped when the general election came round in 1892, they would send him to Parliament in support of the present Government, and might they have another six years reign. They were having Mr. Disraeli first in the Altrincham Division, and they would give him a hand up, and when they had got him there, he hoped they would keep him there. (Applause.) Mr. E. Swanwick seconded, and said he was quite sure the men of High Legh would join with those of Lymm to return Mr. Disraeli with a thumping majority. Mr. Disraeli replied, and proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was carried with accla- mation. The National Anthem was sung, after which three cheers were given for Colonel Legh and Mr. Disraeli.

div.head: AN "ICE CARNIVAL" NEAR WAR-
div.p: AN "ICE CARNIVAL" NEAR WAR-
RINGTON.

A pond lying between the farms of Mr. Warbur- ton and Mr. John Bennett, of Bowsey Old Hall, was the centre of a gay and pleasing scene on Tuesday evening. The ice which covered the pond had been brushed clear of the snow, and° there was assembled upon it a large gathering of friends who had been invited by the families of Mr. Bennett and Mr. Warburton. The pond is interspersed with a large number of willow trees and these were profusely hung with Japanese and Chinese lanterns the varied lights of which gave the spot a brilliant and unusual appearance. Numbers of ladies and gentlemen present glided in and ont amongst the willows on their skates, while home-made sleighs were used by those who did not feel at home on the "irons." Refreshments were sent out at intervals from the farm houses, and when at last the gather- ing dispersed every orie declared that the evening had been spent in an exceedingly pleasant manner.

A Lloyd's despatch says that the steamer Jermnos, from Port Said, has put back to Cardiff from the Barry. Roads, damaged by a collision with the steamer Gwen- doline, of Newport. It is authoritatively announced,says the Press Associa- tion's Taunton correspondent, that the Great Western Railway directors have, in consequence of Colonel Rich's recommendations in his report of the recent disaster at Norton Fitzwarren, ordered the immediate construction of twelve refuge sidings between Exeter and Weston. A landslip which occurred on Thursday at the new tunnel which the London and North-Western Railway Company are making at Marsden buried two men, named respectively Roy and Crabtree. When they were released it was found that both men were very badly injured, and Roy died a few hours after at Huddersfield Infirmary.

div.head: 1890, AND THE WAY OUT.
div.p: 1890, AND THE WAY OUT.
NEW YEAR'S DAY AT WARRINGTON.

The New Year was quietly ushered in at Warring- ton. The severe frost and biting wind of New Year's Eve were strong pe suasives against spending the evening out-of-doors and consequently the streets of the town were very much deserted. Later on a number of people turned out to attend the Watch Night services, which were held in different places of worship, amongst others at Wy- cliffe Church and the Parish Church. At St. John's Presbyterian Church the children of the Sunday School were treated to a waxwork display by their teachers. On New Year's Day shops were opened as usual in the morning, but at noon most of the places of business were closed. During the after- noon the annual treat was given in the Public Hall to a large number of the Old Folks of the town, It is, perhaps, worthy of notice that at the Police Court there was not a single peri,on charged with drunkenness or other offence on the evening previous.

NEW YEAR'S DAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. 'with the advent of the New Year, a thaw set in, and towards noon, the streets were in a state of slush. The hopes of numerous skaters who intended to take advantage of the holiday, by spending the day in skating were thus destroyed. All the places of business and works in the town were closed, Mat the state of the streets under the circumstances were un- usually quiet. The Railway Stations early in the day however were very busy, a large number of people journeying by train to various places. principally Man- chester and Liverpool, the bookings for these places being unusualiy heavy. Work at the Post Offices was again very heavy the number of letters and parcels dealt with being far in excess of previous years. The various Sun- day Schools held their annual treatsto the scholars, when the prizes earned during the year were distributed. Be- low will be found particulars of the whole of the meet- ings referred to. PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. The teachers and elder scholars were entertained to tea in the schoolroom, the younger scholars having been similarly entertained on Friday. Toe tea was of an ex- cellent description, and was heartily enjoyed. After tea those present amused themselves in games, &c., until late in the evening. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL. The children attending the above school to the number of about 250, sat down to an excellently set zed tea in the schoolroom provided by Mrs. King of Earlestown. The wants of the youngsters were attended to by the teachers, and several of the elder scholars, and they ap- peared to thoroughly enjoy the good things set before them. After tea, a pleasing entertainment was held presided over by the Rev. James Allatt. He was glad to say that they had some 110 bound volumes to distribute, and he hoped that these would be a source of pleasure to them in their own homes. Mr. Moses Battersby, secretary of the Sunday school, read the annual report, in which he stated that the average attendance of the teachers was 17, and of the scholars 160. Mr. T. Thompson, in submitting the re- port of the penny bank, stated that during the year the deposits amounted to £lBB 12s. 2d..and the withdrawals to £207. The total number of transactions for the year was 2,478, against 2,697 last year, a decrease of 229, bringing it to about the same total as 1888. An excellent programme was gone through, and was well received. During an interval, Mr. Allatt distributed 110 bound volumes of magazines to the scholars. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. About 330 of the children attending the above school put in an appearance at the annual tea and did ample justice to the edibles provided. The tables were presided over by the teachers, ant several lady members of the congregation. After tea an entertainment was held in the upper room presided over by the Rev. A. P. Walton. The room had been very tastefully decorated for the occasion, and presented a cheerful and pleasing appear- ance. After the meeting which was patronised by a crowded audience, the Secretary Mr. P. Parr, read the 35th annual report, in which he stated that the number of :officers and teachers was 75, average attendance. morning 61 per cent.. afternoon 77, 55 teachers were members of the Wesleyan Methodist Society. Membem of the class, in the schools 33. Scholars on the books 435, being an increase of 34 over 1889. the financial statement showed receipts, including a balance of £l36s. 3P., to be £74105. lli-d.,andexpendi- ture £55 13s. 5d., leaving a balance of £lB 17s. qd. The library in connection with the school contained 701 volumes,, with 28 readers; books issued during the year 562. The Chairman next presented 112 nicely bound books to the children who had been successful in ob- taining an entry into the round "0 "class, which includes those who have not missed a single attendance during the year. A capital programme was then gone through. An address was also given by Mr. J. A. Lee, of the Rev. Charles Garrett's mission, Liverpool. BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL. At this school 250 children sat down to tea, which was presided over by the teachers. Mr. W. Limond, secretary, in his report stated that the school was in a prosperous condition, the present number of scholars on the books being 282, with a staff of 21 teachers and officers. The average attendance of the scholars was 163 per Sunday. The financial statement showed a balance in hand of £ll Bs. 3d. During the evening Mr. F. G. Aveline, a former superintendent of the school, distributed to the scholars 125 prizes for good attendance, conduct and lessons. The rest of the evening was taken up by a magic lantern entertainment, by Mr. J. H. Graham, illustrating the story of" Her Bennie," a number of local and comic sketches were also thrown on the sheet, giv- ing much enjoyment to the youngsters. OrOOD TEMPLAR ANNUAL PARTY. On New Year's Eve, the Earlestown Good Templars held their annual party, when a fair number of members and friends met in the lodg,eroom, Bridge-st. At 9 p.m. a coffee supper was provided, and the usual justice done. This was followed by an entertainment, Bro. George Clarke, D.C., conducting, when a varied and interesting
programme was nicely rendered. The usual Christmas games, &c., followed, and as the year turned, a recess was declared, when the usual hearty congratulations and good wishes were freely expressed.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. THE CAUSE LIST contained the following-4 de- fault summonses, 48 original plaint summonses, and 37 judgment summonses.. CLAIM BY A MANAGER.—George Bee, late manager for Mr. Scott, of the Imperial Tea: Co., Buttermarket-street, sued Mr. Scott for £2 Bs., for wages alleged to be due. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne for the defence. It appeared *from the evidence that defendant asked plaintiff to clean some fruit, and, the latter refusing, defendant told him to put on his coat and go home. Several shop-managers were called, and they stated that it was according to the custom of the trade, the duty of a manager to clean the fruit. His Honour said, that being the case, he must give judg- ment for the defendant.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY:
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY:

A meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterday. The Rei . G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Swinton, Kilshall,. Smith, and Humphries; S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and. F. Ker- foot (inspector). THE PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY.—The SURVEYOR re- ported that as the proposed new Lancashire' Derbyshire and East Coast Railway would run through the Grap- penhall district he wrote to the solicitors asking them to deposit with him a plan of the undertaking. He had examined the plan which was sent and saw nothing that called for any steps to be taken by the Authority in les- pect of the proposed line. THE LIGHTING OF LATCHFORD.—A memorial signed by a number of influential residents in Latchford,and Grap- penhall was read, calling attention to the unlighted and dark state of the road from Latchford station to • Grap- penhall, also the road called Acker's-lane and. a road leading to new property off Acker's-lane,,and asking that lamps should be put up as soon as possible—The CLERK, suggested that the cost of lighting the district immedi- ately outside the borough should be made-a generall charge on the rates of the Authority's district rather than on the districts lighted.—The CHAIR/4A/ asked upon what grounds this suggestion was made.—The CLERM said the people who lived outside the lighted, districts enjoyed some little benefit in passing through,, and be- sides ther was no stating but that at any time' some country town might want to be lighted,. and it would become a v...ey heavy. charge upon that townshipalone. —The CHAIRMAN said he could not seethe justice of mak- ing the ratepayers at Rixten pay for the lighting of Latchford. ( Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. C. Sumon said that it was very likely that under the district Council's-bill which was shortly to be put before Parliament provision would be made for lighting main roads where there wasa. suffi cient population to, justify them, in doing so,. He urged that the Authority should take a broad view ot this question as lighting and other advantages induced people to live outside. the borough, and thus increased the rateable value of the Authority's. district. Ile. was in favour of the cost of lighting being made a. general, district charge.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON said they wont(' be having applications from other townships.—Mr. Swin- TON : We shad have an application from Winwick—Mr. J. C. SUTTON : There will be building in that direction.— Mr. JOHN HOUGHTON said that the ma.nure works would stop building in that dinection.—Mr. J. C. SUTTON : Not of cottage property. Hie also pointed out that the memorialists from Latchford were all heavy ratepayers. —Mr. W. OWEN (surveyor) said he thought ten tamps would be sufficient to light the Latchford district, and for each lamp there woutct be an annual charge of £2 148.—M.r.JoHN HOUGHTON did not think a charge like that would press heavily on the wealthy people of Latchford.—lt was decided that the memorial or the Lighting of Latchford district be referred to. the Streets Committee to report, the question as to whether the cost should be charged on the lighted district alone or on the whole of the Authority's district being left over for fur- ther consideration. A HEALTH RESORT—Dr.. Sephton reported that the death rate for the past month. ha ci been, 8.5 per 1,000, as compared with 12:2 during the last three months, and /1-2 the corresponding month of last year.—The CHAIR- MAN : People will be coming to our district as a health resort.

div.head: MURDER IN LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE MURDER IN LIVERPOOL.

--- Arthur Edward Penfold, who is charged with the murder of a young woman named Margaret Stewart alias Isabella Cowie, was brought before Mr. Raffles at the Liverpool Police Court on Tuesday. At the inquest on the previous day the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder, and the same evidence was now repeated. The prisoner asked no questions from any of the witnesses and had nothing to say in reply to the charge. He wa3 committed for trial.
SHOCKING DEATH OF FOUR YOUTHS.

Four youths were engaged on Monday scaling a boiler at Messrs. Irven Bros'. lard refinery, Liverpool. when. by some mischance, the connection with the next boiler was opened, and the boiling water and steam a poured iu upon them. When recovered their bodies !Presented A terrible spectacle. The victims must have been soficr catad almost instantaneously, as no sounds wer,e hearil• Unsuccessful but gallant attempts were maue by the assistant engineer and another Qmploye to rescue the unfortunate youths. On Wednesday the inquest was had relative to the. deaths of Richard Brown, Edward Price, Edward Mathews, and Thomas Mc'Evoy, four youths Who were killed on Monday at the lard refinery of Messm. irven Brothers in Liverpool. The jury returned a qtrdict of accidental death, and exprel s..Tpathy Witp the parents of the boys and also. 'Mal the, Mon.

div.head: LATEST LATES I NE WS.
div.p: LATEST LATES I NE WS.

CHAIRMAN OF MIDLAND RAILWAY. Yesterday, at a meeting of Midland Railway direc- tors at Derby, Mr. George Ernest Paget was elected chairman. FIVE PERSONS FROZEN TO DEATH. Yesterday a tramp, his wife, and three children were found frozen to death, between West Wratting and Abingdon, on the Cambridge-road. THE FAVERSHAM MURDER, Yesterday, Charles Lvddon was charged on remand at Faversham, with -killing Dr. Lyddon,„ his step- brother by administering morphia. Further evidence was taken. A MANSION DESTROYED BY FIR& Hurstbourne Park, the Hampshire residence of Lord Lyinington, was destroyed by fire on Thursday night, together with its valuable contents, books„ and plate, some furniture only being saved. MR. PARNELL AT AVONDALE; Mr. Parnell arrived at Kingstown yesterday morning, from England, and proceeded to Avondale, whilst he will probably remain some days. Mr. Parnell whilst in Dublin conferred with Mr. Timothy Harringtbn and Dr. Kenny. It is understood that the conference at Boulogne will be resumed on Tuesday next. SKATING COMPETITIONS. The three mile open skating championship race was, at Spalding yesterday, won by George Lee, in ten minutes, thirty-three and three-fifth seconds. At Hun- tingdon, yesterday, open professional mile and half skating race was won by the champion, Jas. Smart, in five minutes, thirty-three and three-fifth seconds. THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE. A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs a decided im provement has again taken place on the North-British Railway, fifty engine-drivers having resumed work yesterday morning, while signalmen throughout the sys, tern are coming in. The Caledonian also state that several men have returned, but the pickets deny this. THE IRISH DIFFICULTY. Mr. Edward Harrington, M.P., arrived home at Tra- lee on Thursday night, and had a public reception. He ad. dressed the crowd, defending his suOpoit of Mr. Parnell and counselling moderation in speaking of Mr. Gladstorth whose assistance, he said, they would yet require la obtaining Home Rule for Ireland, The 'Dublin DaiF Express " says that, before withdrawing nominally for a brief space from the Irish leadership, Mr. Parnell will consult Mr. George Lewis. THE FIRE AT A LEEDS BAZAAR. FIVE DEATHS THIS MORNING. The Press Association's Leeds correspondent telegrilThs that four of the girls injured by the accidental ignition tA their costumes at a Leeds bazaar, on Thursday, ditcl at the infirmary yesterday morning, and it is fearedtbat others will succumb. Eight of them are lying et the infirmary, where the nursing and medical staffs have been most assiduous in their attentions. Four men lifing at Wortley received injuries, which are not seridls, in attempting to put out the burning clothingPf the girls. A later telegram says Maggie Kitchen, another of the injured girls, died in the infirmary yesterday aAerneon. This makes the fifth death.

FATAJ, AcCIDENT AT GOADORNE.—On MOTl•lihy ghOeking fatality occurred- at Evan's colliery; Gol- borne, when it collier named Thomas Regway,resid- ing in Htarcsy-lane, was getting coal. L fall of debris and large stone occurred, completety-burying hn Efforts to extricate him 'alive were made, but it was half an hour before the bcsly could be recovered, Ivhen life wa.s extinct, he being terribly cmshed. Ile was 2&years of age, and leaves a wife and child, The event caused a painful sensation amongst lis fellow workmen. His brother-in-law,, With whcm he wasworking, nearly shared the sue* fate.

On Mcciday a rumour was cirmlated through„Dat St. Helens and district that eleven peoons had been drowned in Eccletton Dam, and that two. men had been drowned at Carl: Will dam. Subseque,nt inquiries of. the police authortles at St, Helens, Prescot, and HayestlK, showed that tii. runcur was withoid tolanclatio,a.
THE BURNING FATALITY AT
WARRINGTON.

On Saturday morning Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest in the Parade Room at the Police Station, as to the death of William Henry Dumbell, four years of age, son of a carter, living at No. 23, Bridgewater-at. The mother, Mary Ann Dumbell, said that on Monday evening last. at 7.30, she lighted a fire in the bedroom, where she remained with her three children, including the deceased, when 80Me one knocked vt the front door ' and she went downstairs to see who was there. She remained downstairs for about ten minutcs when she heard the deceased scream,. She at once ran upstairs, and when she got to'the bedroom door her son ran to her, his nightdress being in flame& She wrapped him in a blanket to put out the flames, and at once sent for Dr. Cannell, who attended her son up to the time of his death, which took place on the following morning at half-past three. All the children were in bed when>she went, downstairs. The deceased, who was the eldest, was not able to explain the cause of the occurrence.. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
WESLEYIN SUNDAY SCHOOL MISSION.

ANNUAL TEA AND GATHERING The annuatea and gathering in connection vrith the Bottermarket-street Wesleyan Sunday :6cllool Mission came off on New Year's Day. The room had been tastefully decorated with curtains, mottoeft &c., for the occasion, by Misses Barlow, Gaukroz'erf A. Ashworth, IV: Ashworth, Vernon, and Lingardt and liessrs. 1.-E. Barlow, J. Ashworth, and J Elli- son, Over 130 persons sat down to tea. Subse-_, .queitly an entertainment prefaced with singing am' prayer, and interspersed with addressesi.was given- Tii6 -spe,kers were the Chairman (the Rev. Thomas Ross), Mr. W. C. Nicholson, Mr. John Barlow, Mr. Gregsononcl- my S. B. Stringer. The following programme was gene. through, Miss Etty Toft acting as accompanist. —Over- ture, Misses Brown and party; song. "The Last Mile. Stone," Miss Bodle ; song, "Captain of the Life Boat,? lir. Frank Burrows.; song, "Come into. the Garden' laud," encore, "Tom Bowling," Mr. Levi Richardson tiong, Miss Figot ; -duet. Richardson ; overture, Misses Brown and party ; recita-' tion, Mr. George Whitfield ; carol, "The Balls," Mission, Choir;. song, Mies Pigot ; song, "The Diver," M. Frank Burrows; song," Home, Dearest Home," encore,. "Daddy," Miss Bodld,; Doxology.—The Secretary,3o.: I. & Barlow, read his annual report. He stated that the Sunday School was progressing satisfactorily ;24 of thy sclulars were enrolled nembers of society and regularlti met in class. There were 183 scholars on therbooks (70 males and 113 females): In the Band of Hope branch of the school, which branch had only existed five weeks,' there were 50 members. The membership of the Society class was 39. The-Saturday evening concerts eantinued to be appreciated, being well attended. The Committee' had, owing to the severe cold, and considering,. that &• large number of people would be thrown out of•empler ment, considered the-desirability of giving a fretediener to all the deserving poor in the neighbourheod. - (pities were made, and lb was discovered that.tstrah undertakinp,cr.woultl be an act of charity,and, so as not t°' interfere with other7similar objects, it was decided te give a free dinner lathe-school on Saturday, Detember. 28th. Without unduly burdening anybody, money an° gifts of fruit, potatoes, &C., were solicited, and thlealr peals responded to very-generously; and the committee were enabled to give to over 300 adults and chibiren substantial•ditmer.,--cnnsisting of potato pie, plum•pud ding, and buns, to the evident pleasure of all present As to the committee's financial position they had alwaY been able to meet current expenses, but during thepast year an unusual outlay had been incurred throughtcer-' tam n slight alterations having been necessary at -the school. The committee hoped to raise the amount: i'et• the debt on this account in a short time, but appeare"' for small donations in aid of that object. The committee in conclusion, stated • that the mission work as a • was showing signs, of renewed vigoer and energy. 'rho • usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings. •

COAL MitilE.3. CASE AT Sr. HELENS. At the Police Court, on Monday, Henry Atherton, C. Ross-st., Edwards Briars, Elephant-lane, and Jafnes• Molyneux, Elephant-lame, colliers,were summoned at the: instance of the Sutton Heath and Lea Green Collier,' Company for a breach a the Coal Mines Regulation Mt' by failing to set sufficient sprags and holing props.ie' Sutton Heath Colliery. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted, and, Mr. Riley defended.. ligr. Swift said the firm felt bound in the interests of their workpeople themselves to enforce' the rules, which provided that colliers should sprag,and prop their working • phces, but it was an unfortunate' matter that•rases had to be brought before the court' over and over again in which men were charged with carelessness, which frequently resulted in injury to theno.' 'selves —Thomas Peruthlgton, certificated manager, gave evidence in support ofthe charge, and, in answer to Mr., Riley, said that up to, a few weeks ago, until the Ante& Union interfered,, the firm was fining the men halF4,l' crown a week whefr they did wrong.—Mr. Riley fJ Mau' when the union threatened to prosecute, you stopped-the fining? Witness ::Yes, I was bound to do so.-14.• Riley : And the first chance you get you send the sunt-1 tnonses in to members of the union? Witness: Y;," because they. are breaking the law.—Mr. Riley contencliw that the case was a disgraceful prosecution on the pot of the employersi. and should be contemptuously. missed. The defence was that the working place .of men was perfectly safe on the day in question, and, that sufficient sprags and props were set. They had worked under similar circumstances without any complaint-for. the past two years. The bench imposed a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs upon each defendant.

QOUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENER A.L QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER. will be holden at the Castle of Chester, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the sth day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Cheater District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury tor the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the sth day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. WHEREAS at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at Nether Knutsford. in and for the County of Chester, on Monday, the 13th day of October, 1890. a Provisional Order was made in the words following, that is to say— At the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace of our Lady the Queen holden at Nether Knutsford, in and for the Countyof Chester, on Monday, the 13th day of October, 1890. WHEREAS a proposal in writing, dated the 13th Stptem- ber, 1890, bath been laid before this Court under the hands of the Honourable Cecil Thomas Parker, Benjamin Chaffers Roberts, Esquire, John Thompson, Esquire, James Sweten- ham, Esquire, and The Reverend Edward Augustus Pitcairn Campbell, five of Her Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Chester, to vary the existing boundaries of the Highway District of the Western Division of the Hundred of Broxton by including within such District and adding thereto the Township of Huntington, in the said County of Chester. NOW IT IS ORDERED by this Court, upon consideration of such proposal, that the said Township of Huntington shall, from and after the 25th day of March. 1891, be added to and form part of the said Highway District of the Western Division of the Hundred of Broxton, in the said County. for all the purposes ot the Highway Acts. AND IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the said Township of Huntington shall be entitled to elect one Waywarden to form part of the Highway Board for the said Highway District. AND IT IS ALSO FURTHER ORDERED that the said Township of limiting- ton so included in such Highway District as aforesaid, shall not be liable to contribute to any Debts or Loans contracted by the said Highway Board for such Highway District prior to the said 25th day of March, 1891. AND THIS COURT (loth hereby appoint the General Quarter Sessions of the Peaco to be held at CHESTER CASTLE, in and for the said County of Chester, on MONDAY, the sth day of January, 1891, for the purpose of taking into considerati6n the Confirmation of the Pro- , . visional Order hereby made. ' NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN, that the Confirma- tion of the said Provisional Order by a Final Order will be taken into consideration by the Justices at the Court of General Quarter Sessions to be held at CHESTER CAST! E aforesaid, on MONDAY, the sth day of January THE COURT will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNDSDAY, the 7th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in (lie Forenoon. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow,Macelesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford 'District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 7th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 16th December, 1890.
